#193. How to be more productive: 6 tips to help you get things done

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1494 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm

How to be more productive: 6 tips to help you get things done

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Industry observers note that you start your day with a proposal: clear your to-do list, get ahead, maybe even sign off early.
  • According to recent reports, busyness and productivity can look identical from the outside, but they’re not the same.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Industry observers note that you start your day with a proposal: clear your to-do list, get ahead, maybe even sign off early. Instead, your attention gets pulled in every direction. Back-to-back calls, a stream of emails, countless tabs open at once. Next thing you know, the day's almost over, your list is still full, and you're left wondering how you’re supposed to get anything done.

According to recent reports, busyness and productivity can look identical from the outside, but they’re not the same. You can stay busy all day tackling small, urgent-feeling tasks without ever touching the work that really counts. Being productive means doing the tasks that matter, which requires staying intentional about where your time and energy go.

So what's getting in the way of your productivity, and what can you do about it? Here’s a closer look at the everyday friction that can slow you down, plus a few shifts to help you make the most of each day.

According to recent reports, most productivity drains are minor, routine points of friction that are easy to miss, yet they add up fast. A few usual suspects:.

Context switching: Research indicates that every jump between tasks costs you the time it takes to mentally reset, even when it feels instant.

Constant interruptions: Responding to notifications and drop-in requests can feel productive, but it turns your attention to other people's priorities.

Unclear priorities: When everything feels urgent, you often default to whatever's quickest instead of what matters most.

Running on empty: Skipping breaks seems like it saves time, but it slows you down later and wears down your focus.

Procrastination: When a task feels overwhelming or unclear, it’s tempting to reach for something more manageable instead of starting the job you need to do.

Recent findings suggest that good news: you can reduce these points of friction without turning your whole day upside down. The tips below aren’t a set system, just a few ideas you can implement on your own terms. Start with one or two, and notice what feels different.

It has been revealed that decide what would make today count before you open your inbox. Not five things, just one that matters most. Write it down somewhere visible, then dedicate the first stretch of your day to that task before anything else pulls your focus away.

💙 Start your day mindfully with this Finding Focus practice on Calm.

In a recent development, multitasking may feel efficient, but your brain can’t really do two things at once. It's switching fast between them, and each switch costs you a little focus and energy. Over a full day, those costs add up.

It has been revealed that try working in single-task blocks. Close the extra tabs, silence your phone, and stay with one task until it's done or you hit a natural stopping point. You'll often finish faster than if you’d juggled three tasks at once.

💙 Learn more with Jay Shetty’s Settle Down by Single-Tasking session on Calm.

Industry observers note that the apps and platforms you use are built to stretch your attention in a dozen directions. Every ping invites you to switch tasks, and you’re driven to take the bait without thinking twice.

You don't have to go off-grid to take back control. Check your email at two or three set times instead of leaving it open. Turn off notifications you don't need, and put your phone in another room during focused work. If one site keeps tempting you, a browser blocker can hold the line.

💙 Explore Digital Distractions from the 7 Days of Focus series on Calm.

Your focus isn't a tap you can leave running. If you push too long without pausing, your attention frays, mistakes creep in, and even small tasks can start to feel hard.

Try working in stretches of about 25 minutes, then step away to stretch, breathe, or look out a window. It’s also worth protecting your downtime in the evenings and on weekends, so you're not completely drained by mid-week.

In a recent development, 💙 Dr. Alex Pang makes the case for smarter rest in The Power of Rest, a Calm masterclass.

In a recent development, your to-do list is probably a mix of very different kinds of work. A report needs deep focus. A stack of emails or calls may not need any. Some work requires creativity, while some mainly requires attention to detail. Tackling tasks in a random order means starting cold, over and over.

According to recent reports, but if you batch similar tasks, you can move through them while you're already warmed up for that type of work. Keep your quick replies to a couple of set windows instead of scattered across the day, and stack your calls so they run one after another. Once you're in the groove of one kind of work, staying there beats starting over.

Recent findings suggest that A task tends to stretch to fill whatever time you give it. Timeboxing flips that. You pick a task, decide up front how long it gets—say 30 minutes—then stop when the time runs out, whether you're finished or not. That cap keeps one email from swallowing a whole morning, and stops you from polishing something long past the point of diminishing returns.

It also takes the guesswork out of what comes next, since you've chosen in advance. Block the slot on your calendar and set a timer. When the box closes, decide consciously whether the task gets another round.

💙 If starting is the hardest part, these 9 techniques can help you stop procrastinating.

It has been revealed that you can train yourself to be more productive by gradually incorporating new helpful habits, like choosing a top priority for the day, single-tasking, and reducing digital distractions. Start with one small change and repeat it until it feels natural. One well-known study found that a new behavior took an average of 66 days to feel automatic—ranging from 18–254 days depending on the person—so give yourself time to adjust.

Industry observers note that yes, people with ADHD often struggle with productivity, and it’s not about effort or willpower. ADHD involves differences in executive function, the mental skills you use to start tasks, strategy, and hold attention. This is why even starting tasks you want to do can feel difficult. The strategies in this article are still useful, though you may need to adapt them to what works for your brain.

💙 If ADHD is getting in the way of your work, here’s more on why that happens and how to deal with it.

Productivity peacocking is when you put more energy into looking busy than into doing meaningful work. Think replying to messages instantly instead of finishing the task at hand, or reorganizing your to-do list for the third time instead of crossing items off.

There's no single best time of day to work, since it depends on your body clock and when your energy naturally rises. Instead of trying to follow someone else's schedule, notice when you feel most alert, and dedicate that window to your most demanding work.

Yes, it's possible to be more productive without working longer hours, since a lot of time gets lost to switching tasks and reacting to interruptions. Try protecting focused blocks, sticking to one task at a time, and taking proper breaks, since a tired brain works slowly and rest can help you get more done.

According to recent reports, stress affects productivity by making it harder to focus, blueprint, and think clearly. When you're stressed, your brain pulls resources away from the areas that handle focus and memory. Bring your stress down and calm your mind with a few minutes of slow breathing.

Sources indicate that one of the most effective ways to stop getting distracted while working is to remove the distraction before you start. Silence notifications, close the extra tabs, and place your phone out of reach so you're not relying on willpower in the moment. When your mind wanders anyway, and it will, bring it back without giving yourself a hard time.

It has been revealed that yes, meditation can help you be more productive, though the effect is indirect. In one randomized study, a two-week mindfulness course improved people's working memory and reduced how often their minds wandered mid-task.

You don't need long sessions, and even a few minutes a day of focusing your attention on your breath works the same mental muscle you use to stay on track while working.

💙 Learn how mindfulness can sharpen your focus with our guide to meditation for productivity.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#192. Why Shame Matters in Politics

Why Shame Matters in Politics

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • In the November 2026 American midterm elections, campaign advertisements were relentless.
  • It has been revealed that the quantity of messages was startling, but so was their content, which frequently transgressed the bounds of decorum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In the November 2026 American midterm elections, campaign advertisements were relentless. Across broadcast television and digital media, a record 573.2 and 500 million dollars were spent on Texas and Ohio campaigns, respectively.[1] Americans received a combined 60 billion political text messages, an average of 170 messages per person.[2].

It has been revealed that the quantity of messages was startling, but so was their content, which frequently transgressed the bounds of decorum. Many campaigns involved insults and unsubstantiated rumors, meant to undermine the credibility of candidates.[3] These were cases of mudslinging—the exchange of personal insults or abuse, especially unjust ones, to damage the reputation of an opponent.[4] While the delivery of unsolicited messages directly to our iPhones was a novel experience, mudslinging itself is not a upcoming American phenomenon.

It has been revealed that for example, in the 1796 U.S. presidential election, John Adams and his supporters called Thomas Jefferson an atheist, and Jefferson’s supporters referred to Adams as “His Rotundity” and an “old, querulous, bald, crippled, toothless Adams.”[5] In the presidential election of 1828, Democrats accused John Quincy Adams of the misuse of public funds, and Whigs attacked Andrew Jackson’s military record and character.[6].

There are helpful ways to criticize a political opponent in an election. Examples include drawing attention to a poor track record of leadership or patterns of equivocation in policy statements. But personal vitriol, fabricated attacks, and ridicule are not among them. Mudslinging is often at odds with virtues such as charity and honesty. It distracts from substantive policy conversations. When a candidate campaigns in this way, he has shown himself to be undiscerning, cruel, and sometimes shameless.

To be shameless is to avoid moral censure or be unapologetic in wrongdoing. The shameless person intentionally flouts moral norms—doing the wrong thing, even though he knows better. Alternatively, he may be unaware of moral norms—even though he should have known better. In either case, the shameless person is blameworthy yet fails to experience the sting of a moral sanction.

According to recent reports, I provided a recent example of shamelessness in American civic life—campaigns built around dishonesty and personal vitriol. But shamelessness is not just a problem during election cycles. It is a problem in daily governance, such as when leaders demean others or abuse power for personal gain. It is a problem on social media, where people overshare personal information and make inappropriate jokes. And shamelessness is a problem in corporate America. Examples include fraud, bribery, and flagrant violations of environmental protections.

So, why does shame matter in politics? Here are three reasons.

Shame is a negative-valence, self-conscious emotion, characterized by a critical self-evaluation.[7] It construes oneself as problematic. Shame is not an emotion that people like to experience. It is popularly regarded as “guilt’s ugly sister” and a disposable emotion.[8] We would rather do away with shame entirely than feel bad about ourselves. However, it is probably not a coincidence that a culture that wishes to dispose of shame is also riddled with shamelessness. If we are not sensitive to wrongdoing, how can we be expected to act well?

Sources indicate that A better (albeit more challenging) approach is to recover shame in healthy forms. This is the approach we take with other misdirected emotions. An example is that, when a child throws a tantrum, we do not regard her anger as disposable or inherently unproductive. We educate this emotion toward its proper end, helping the child to experience anger in fitting ways.

In a recent development, I defined shame in terms of a global negative self-evaluation. This distinguishes shame from guilt, which attends to particular bad actions. Tangney (1998) puts it this way: Shame claims, “I did that terrible thing,” whereas guilt says, “I did that terrible thing.” In some cases, shame’s self-evaluation makes it less action-guiding, since shame, unlike guilt, does not see a particular wrongdoing to repair. However, shame’s construal of the person means the emotion can better recognize patterns of bad action.

According to recent reports, additionally, shame attends to considerations of moral beauty or fineness—features of the moral life which are not neatly captured in terms of ‘good’ and ‘bad’.[9] Finally, shame attends to social standing and relational repair.[10] It aids our sensitivity to the feelings and expectations of others. Without shame, we lack the vision it provides, which helps us navigate the complexities of the moral life.

Sources indicate that imagine you have a rule in your home: no jumping on the couches. But you don’t enforce the rule. Maybe you see the child jumping, and instead of scolding him, you turn away or smile. The child may jump on the couch tentatively at first. Eventually he will jump freely and shamelessly, unconcerned about the rule that apparently does not apply to him.

Shame matters because it holds a leader to a standard and keeps the standard emotionally salient. This is vital because it reduces the likelihood of bad actions. It also reduces the tendency toward assumptions of norm-differentiation in leadership—acting as though rules, in general, do not apply.

Sources indicate that finally, shame matters because we are imitative creatures. We can tell young people that moral character matters, but when those in authority are uncivil and unapologetic, or shameless in how they comport themselves in public, this is the lesson that stays with them.

#191. Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health

📅 10 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (660 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health

📅 10 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that loneliness and social isolation are widespread in the United States.
  • Until recently, however, researchers had little idea how many years of good health might actually be lost to loneliness and social isolation.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at Tulane University's Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine have now attempted to put a number on that toll.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that loneliness and social isolation are widespread in the United States. According to a 2023 report, about half of U.S. adults experience loneliness, while nearly as many are socially isolated. Despite health consequences that can rival other major risk factors, both problems remain relatively overlooked as urgent public health concerns.

Until recently, however, researchers had little idea how many years of good health might actually be lost to loneliness and social isolation.

Loneliness Linked to Fewer Healthy Years.

It has been revealed that researchers at Tulane University's Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine have now attempted to put a number on that toll. Their first-of-its-kind observational study, published in Nature Communications, found that loneliness and social isolation were associated with the loss of nearly six years of life free from mental disorders such as depression and anxiety. The effects on physical health were smaller, but still significant.

In a recent development, "Overall, the study found that social isolation and loneliness can have a significant impact on disease-free life expectancy," noted lead author Lu Qi, HCA Regents Distinguished Chair and professor in Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine at Tulane. "This includes both physical and mental disease.".

Industry observers note that although loneliness and social isolation are often treated as the same thing in everyday conversation, researchers distinguish between them. Social isolation refers to an objective lack of social connections. Loneliness, by contrast, describes a person's subjective dissatisfaction with the quality of their relationships, regardless of how many social interactions they actually have.

"The findings weren't surprising to me," Qi stated. "Previous studies found that social isolation and loneliness are related to mortality, especially premature mortality, and this study provides additional evidence.".

Tracking More Than 277,000 Adults.

According to recent reports, the researchers analyzed data from 277,489 adults between the ages of 40 and 69. At the beginning of the study, none had seven major chronic conditions: diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, dementia, cancer, depression and anxiety.

Using age 50 as a reference point, the team calculated how loneliness and social isolation were associated with the number of years participants could expect to live without these diseases.

Compared with people who experienced neither loneliness nor social isolation, women experiencing both had 2.4 fewer years free from physical disease. Men experiencing both had 1.7 fewer years.

Sources indicate that the difference was even larger for mental health. Women experiencing both loneliness and social isolation lived about 3.7 fewer years without mental disorders, while men lived approximately 5.8 fewer years free from those conditions.

"This comes down to the gender differences between men and women," Qi noted. "Our research found men are more susceptible to being affected by loneliness. We also know that women tend to live longer than men. There are gender advantages with certain diseases.".

Healthy Habits Help With Isolation, but Not Loneliness.

It has been revealed that the researchers also examined whether lifestyle could alter these associations. Healthier habits, including better diet, regular exercise, sufficient sleep, and not smoking, measurably reduced the loss of disease-free years associated with social isolation.

In a recent development, loneliness produced a different pattern. A healthier lifestyle did not significantly reduce the additional health risks linked to feeling lonely. That distinction suggests loneliness and social isolation may require different approaches when it comes to protecting health.

The research team looks to study additional population groups in the future and use clinical trials to investigate whether loneliness and social isolation directly cause the health effects observed in the study.

#189. Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1556 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley

Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding love is major business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business.
  • According to recent reports, the promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages.
  • According to recent reports, as a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding love is major business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

According to recent reports, the promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app customers to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

According to recent reports, as a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

Sources indicate that so if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

According to recent reports, what about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

It has been revealed that perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user notes they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

It has been revealed that with the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

An alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

Recent findings suggest that amie M. Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles.
  • That’s just your teens becoming independent.
  • Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

That’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science highlights this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:.

None of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

It has been revealed that Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he claims he doesn’t care. What should I do?

Recent findings suggest that A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” claims Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” says Bronk.

According to recent reports, to help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

“While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” says Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more quickly identify a purposeful direction.”.

Recent findings suggest that research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, says Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a big challenge.

Instead of trying to manage their path, says Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

Industry observers note that “This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she notes. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Recent findings suggest that taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

Finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” indicates Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”.

Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that “I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” claims Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”.

Chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

Sources indicate that “There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” states Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”.

It has been revealed that that stated, spending time with family is also vital. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

Recent findings suggest that only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an matter, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

Industry observers note that one last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, says Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, notes Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

That noted, it’s still important for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

In a recent development, Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, claims Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

Allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” says Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”.

It has been revealed that as Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

Industry observers note that trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, says Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

If sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” claims Farber. “It helps people find a latest narrative when they’re stuck.”.

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, claims Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

Sources indicate that to help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, indicates Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

Recent findings suggest that and as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” says Bibby.

Industry observers note that Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

It has been revealed that people turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, says Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”.

In her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”.

In a recent development, read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

It has been revealed that to that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is fresh to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

Industry observers note that it also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin claims.

#187. What is languishing? Meaning, signs, and how to cope

📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1869 w)

What is languishing? Meaning, signs, and how to cope

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Mental health struggles aren’t always obvious to the people experiencing them.
  • Basically, languishing is the state of mind between depression and flourishing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Mental health struggles aren’t always obvious to the people experiencing them. Sometimes, you might just feel… stuck. You’re not exactly sad, but you’re not happy either. You’re not falling apart, but you’re definitely not thriving. That feeling is called languishing, and it’s more common than you think.

Basically, languishing is the state of mind between depression and flourishing. It’s that foggy middle ground where life feels muted.

In a recent development, and while languishing might not seem like a big deal, if you ignore it, it can quietly erode your sense of joy and purpose. That’s why it’s so important to understand what languishing is and explore ways to lift the fog and feel more connected to yourself again.

In a recent development, languishing is the emotional equivalent of treading water. You’re not drowning, but you’re not moving forward either. You’re just floating, tired, and maybe even a little numb.

On the mental health spectrum, languishing falls somewhere between depression and flourishing — and it can come on so subtly that you don’t even realize it’s happening. If you’re languishing, you might struggle to concentrate or feel “meh” more days than not. You might not be able to remember the last time something excited you, or just have a general feeling of going through the motions without any real sense of meaning.

And because languishing doesn’t always feel like a problem that needs solving, it can be easy to ignore. Don’t. If it’s left unchecked, languishing can lead to deeper mental health challenges over time.

It has been revealed that languishing may seem similar to depression, burnout, and anxiety, but they’re different in key ways. Here’s how:.

In a recent development, depression: Depression is usually deeper and heavier than languishing. It can include persistent sadness, hopelessness, and a loss of pleasure in everything. You may also feel disconnected from yourself or others in a way that requires clinical care.

Sources indicate that burnout: Typically, burnout comes from chronic stress. It leads to emotional exhaustion, cynicism, and a sense of being overwhelmed. Languishing can overlap with burnout, but it’s usually broader, affecting your energy in all areas of life.

According to recent reports, anxiety: Anxiety is often high-energy and fear-based. It can show up as worry, racing thoughts, or a sense of dread. On the other hand, languishing feels flat.

According to recent reports, languishing can slowly build, dulling your emotional energy. Here are some reasons why it happens:.

Chronic stress: Nonstop work pressure or caregiving can wear down your nervous system.

Disconnection: Not feeling connected to meaning can make your life feel empty or purposeless.

Prolonged uncertainty: Global unrest or personal instability can leave you emotionally worn out.

Lack of novelty: Doing the same thing day after day can cause your brain to check out from boredom.

Isolation: Lack of meaningful interactions can make you feel unseen or untethered.

Industry observers note that if you’ve been feeling off without knowing why, you could be experiencing languishing. Here are five signs:.

You’re coasting: You’re showing up and ticking boxes, but it all feels mechanical. You feel disconnected from any real sense of drive or direction.

Flow feels out of reach: Things you used to lose yourself in, like reading, creating, laughing, and dancing, have lost their appeal. You’re finding it hard to immerse yourself in anything, no matter how meaningful it once felt.

In a recent development, your motivation has disappeared: Small plans you used to get excited about—like a weekend walk or trying a new recipe—now feel like uphill climbs. It takes more effort, and there’s less satisfaction.

Your emotions feel muted: You’re not experiencing intense sadness necessarily, but you’re also not feeling much else. It’s also harder to feel joy and excitement when things are going well.

Time feels strange: Days feel like they blend together, and you feel like you’re in a fog.

It has been revealed that languishing can make it hard to change things up and rebuild. But all change, no matter how significant or small, starts with just one step. That’s all you have to do — one teeny step at a time.

Here are 10 small but meaningful ways to slowly begin moving forward.

In a recent development, saying “I think I’m languishing” can bring a surprising sense of relief. It creates space between you and the experience.

It tells you that you’re not lazy, broken, or dramatic. You’re just in a tough emotional patch. Naming it gives you power, and it reminds you that this is a state, not a character flaw.

Read more: 10 mindfulness questions to help you check in with yourself.

When you’re languishing, trying to feel great can backfire. Your goal should be to reconnect with anything that feels nourishing—like a song or a hot shower—not to feel endlessly inspired.

Start with where you are and slowly shift your internal goalposts from “thriving” to “engaged enough to care again.”.

Here are 10 ways to reconnect with yourself if you’re feeling off right now.

In a recent development, flow is that magical zone where you’re so absorbed in something that time disappears. You don’t have to lose hours. Just five to 10 minutes of doing something immersive can help to light you up again.

Recent findings suggest that try cooking a familiar recipe while listening to music or watering your plants, and notice how they’ve changed. You could also play a game on your phone that feels satisfying.

💙 Listening to Flow with Tamara Levitt can help you find yours.

Rigid routines can feel impossible when you’re low on energy, but a little structure helps.

Anchoring yourself with a morning stretch, a mid-day walk around the block, or a journaling session before bed might be just what you need to start feeling more like yourself.

Read more: 6 best morning stretches to wake up & start the day right.

We tend to isolate when we’re languishing, but connection, even in tiny doses, can be one of the most effective antidotes. Consider sending a “thinking of you” message to someone you love or exchanging a friendly “hello” with your local barista.

Refocusing your attention can make you feel more centered.

Try turning off your phone while you eat a meal, reading a book for 10 minutes straight, or even concentrating on one movie instead of flipping between highlights.

According to recent reports, get back into a hobby, a place, or a type of music you used to love. It may not be inspiring right away, and that’s okay. Many times, the action leads to the emotion.

Simple, restorative movement can help shift your mental energy, even subtly.

Try stretching in bed before you get up, doing a few yoga poses, or just taking your next phone call while standing.

💙 Get your blood pumping during this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah.

According to recent reports, good enough is fine. Eat the frozen meal, ignore the dishes, or wear the same sweatshirt two days in a row. You don’t have to be impressive. You just have to be kind to yourself. Here are 10 ways to cultivate more self-kindness in your life.

In a recent development, you’re allowed not to be okay. If that’s the case, consider reaching out to a professional to see if they can help you get to the root cause of your emotions.

Industry observers note that if asking for help feels too hard, try reaching out to a trusted friend. You could simply start by saying, “Hey, I’m not doing great. Can we talk soon?” or “I’m feeling off lately, and I just need someone to listen.”.

Recent findings suggest that tiredness typically has a clear cause—like maybe you didn’t sleep well—and once you rest, the tiredness goes away. On the other hand, languishing persists even after you get some sleep or take time off.

Sources indicate that unlike simple exhaustion, languishing is an emotional and mental dullness that makes everything feel like a chore. If you’re waking up after a full night’s rest and still feeling apathetic or disconnected, you could be languishing.

In a recent development, there isn’t an official test for languishing, because it isn’t a clinical diagnosis. Researchers use a 14-question survey, developed by sociologist Corey Keyes, to sort people into languishing, moderate, or flourishing mental health. It’s built for research, so it can’t diagnose you.

For a quick self-check, ask yourself:.

Have most days felt flat or foggy for weeks?

Is it hard to feel interested in things you used to enjoy?

Does the feeling stay even after you rest?

If you noted yes to several, you may be languishing. If you’re unsure, a doctor or mental health professional can help.

Languishing isn’t a clinical diagnosis, but that doesn’t mean it’s not real or crucial. Languishing is what psychologists call a “subclinical” state. This means that it doesn’t meet the criteria for mental illness, but it’s still a sign that your mental health needs attention.

Languishing is your brain’s version of a check engine light. It’s telling you that something’s off.

Languishing and depression can feel alike, so look at how heavy the feeling is and how it affects your days. When you’re languishing, you can usually keep up with daily life, but everything feels flat or foggy.

Depression goes deeper. It often brings hopelessness or feelings of worthlessness, and it can make daily tasks like working or sleeping hard.

Industry observers note that if your mood is getting heavier, hasn’t lifted in several weeks, or you feel hopeless, talk to a doctor or mental health professional. If you can’t tell which one you’re dealing with, that’s reason enough to ask. Mindfulness can help with languishing, but it’s not a replacement for care.

Languishing isn’t another word for an existential crisis, but they can overlap. An existential crisis usually involves questioning the meaning of life, your purpose, or your place in the world. It tends to be philosophical and emotionally intense.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, languishing is more like emotional white noise. Instead of asking, “What’s the point of it all?” You tend to ask,  “Why don’t I care about anything right now?”.

That stated, languishing can often trigger bigger questions about meaning and direction, especially if it lingers.

According to recent reports, languishing can last anywhere from a few weeks to several months, depending on your circumstances and support system. Sometimes it can fade on its own, especially if your environment changes or if you start naturally reconnecting with things that bring you energy. But often, it sticks around until you intervene.

If you’d like to stop feeling this way, small shifts in connection, movement, attention, and routine can start to turn the tide. The key is to treat it seriously, even if it feels subtle, because you deserve to feel alive again.

#186. After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease

📅 13 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal.
  • Sources indicate that alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate.
  • In a recent development, the drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. The treatment, called Zanvastro, represents a major advance for patients who previously had no options beyond managing their symptoms.

Sources indicate that alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate. Zanvastro is the first and only approved disease-modifying treatment for the condition, meaning it targets an underlying biological process responsible for the disease rather than simply relieving its effects.

In a recent development, the drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Much of that work took place in the laboratory of Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences and former director of the Waisman Center, whose discoveries helped make the treatment possible. Ionis Pharmaceuticals collaborated in developing the drug.

According to recent reports, clinical trials offered encouraging results. Patients receiving Zanvastro generally experienced stabilization of their motor function, and some indicated improvements in their ability to move.

"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," Messing says.

Alexander Disease: A Rare and Devastating Brain Disorder.

Alexander disease affects fewer than one in every million people worldwide. Although exceptionally uncommon, its consequences can be severe, with symptoms that gradually interfere with everyday activities and essential bodily functions.

People with the disorder may develop seizures, lose previously acquired developmental abilities, experience increasing difficulty walking or moving, and struggle with speaking or swallowing. Some also develop dangerously elevated pressure inside the brain.

The disease does not follow a single predictable course. Symptoms may first emerge during infancy, childhood, or adulthood, and their severity and progression can differ depending on when the condition begins.

For decades, doctors could offer supportive care and treatments to ease individual symptoms, but they had no approved medication capable of targeting the disease itself.

An Unexpected Discovery Revealed the Genetic Cause.

Sources indicate that the breakthrough can be traced to research Messing conducted with Michael Brenner, professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In the late 1990s, their work identified the genetic changes responsible for Alexander disease, providing scientists with a specific biological target for developing treatments.

The discovery began with an unexpected result in laboratory mice.

Sources indicate that messing and Brenner had genetically engineered mice to produce unusually high amounts of a protein known as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This protein is normally found in astrocytes, specialized cells that help support and maintain healthy function in the brain and spinal cord.

Sources indicate that to the researchers' surprise, the modified mice developed abnormal protein deposits throughout their brains. These deposits appeared inside astrocytes and closely resembled the distinctive abnormalities seen in people with Alexander disease.

"We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease," Messing states.

The abnormal deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a defining characteristic of the disorder. Additional genetic studies involving people diagnosed with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the gene responsible for producing GFAP were the underlying cause.

"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy -- the GFAP protein," Messing explains.

Sources indicate that identifying the genetic cause also made diagnosing the condition much simpler. Instead of relying on invasive brain biopsies to look for characteristic tissue abnormalities, doctors could use genetic testing from a blood sample to identify the mutations associated with the disease.

Scientists Develop a Drug That Targets Harmful Protein Buildup.

Once researchers understood the role of GFAP, their next challenge was finding a way to reduce its production and prevent damaging levels of the protein from accumulating in brain cells.

Messing joined forces with Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, to create improved rodent models of Alexander disease. These models more closely reproduced key features of the disorder, giving scientists a way to investigate potential treatments before testing them in people.

The team focused on a straightforward idea: If excessive GFAP contributes to the disease, lowering the amount produced might help protect the nervous system.

In collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the researchers pursued a technology known as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs).

In a recent development, these treatments use short, specially designed pieces of genetic material to interfere with instructions that cells use to manufacture particular proteins. Rather than targeting every protein in a cell, an ASO can be designed to reduce production of a specific one.

For Alexander disease, that target was GFAP.

The experimental treatment produced promising results in rodents, supporting the decision to move forward with human testing. A clinical trial began in the summer of 2021.

Zanvastro uses this same targeted strategy. By limiting GFAP production, the drug aims to reduce the buildup of the protein before it can cause additional damage.

Industry observers note that because the treatment needs to reach the central nervous system, it is administered through an injection into the spinal canal. A trained healthcare professional gives the injection once every three months.

Clinical Trials Show Improvements in Walking and Movement.

The human trial provided evidence that lowering GFAP could offer meaningful benefits to people living with Alexander disease.

Ionis Pharmaceuticals conducted the international study across 13 clinical sites, enrolling 54 patients to evaluate the treatment's safety and effectiveness.

After receiving Zanvastro for a little more than a year, treated patients demonstrated significantly better walking speeds than patients who had not received the drug.

According to recent reports, the results also indicated that treatment could stabilize motor function, an vital outcome for a progressive disorder that can steadily undermine a person's ability to move independently. Some participants experienced improvements in motor performance.

These findings helped establish Zanvastro as the first treatment approved to modify the underlying disease process in Alexander disease, rather than focusing exclusively on symptom relief.

The FDA approval covers people with Alexander disease across the full age spectrum, from infancy through adulthood.

In a recent development, zanvastro is expected to become available in the United States in the weeks following the approval. Outside the United States, access to the drug will be handled through a licensing agreement between Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Recordati, a major pharmaceutical firm headquartered in Italy.

A 30-Year Scientific Journey Offers New Hope.

For Messing and his colleagues, the approval represents the culmination of more than 30 years of research, beginning with basic investigations into brain cell biology and eventually leading to a treatment for patients.

What started as an unexpected finding in genetically modified mice helped reveal the cause of an extremely rare disease, transformed how doctors diagnose it, and provided the foundation for developing a drug.

The achievement is also an example of translational research, the process of turning discoveries made in laboratories into treatments that can directly benefit patients.

Throughout that journey, individuals living with Alexander disease and their families played an essential role by supporting the research and participating in studies.

"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," Messing states.

#185. Has the Most Wonderful Moment of Your Life Already Happened?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (601 w)

Has the Most Wonderful Moment of Your Life Already Happened?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • In a recent newsletter, Jack Maden, the founder and writer of Philosophy Break, was asked about ideas that changed how he sees the world.
  • For Hanh, this is not about looking back on our lives through a upcoming lens that highlights what we may not have appreciated then.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

In a recent newsletter, Jack Maden, the founder and writer of Philosophy Break, was asked about ideas that changed how he sees the world. He cited the Vietnamese Buddhist philosopher Thich Nhat Hanh, who posed the question that is in the title: Has the most wonderful moment of your life already happened?

For Hanh, this is not about looking back on our lives through a upcoming lens that highlights what we may not have appreciated then. No, for Hanh, the most wonderful moment of our lives may already have happened, because for him, every moment has the capacity baked into it to be that wonderful moment, but it eludes us because we’re too preoccupied to notice it. What most of us do is put our hope in the future: the “when we’s—graduate, get married, have a child—or the “only if’s—make a million dollars, get that promotion—etc. By not being mindful in the present and instead dwelling mentally on the past or future, both the opportunity and the awareness of the wonderfulness of now slip right by.

The psychology of mindfulness is, of course, well known, thanks not only to Buddhism but also to writers like Eckhart Tolle and his book The Power of Now. While Tolle does a good job, in my mind, of helping us realize that the now is all we have, all we can live in, I agree with Maden that Hanh’s question offers a different, positive, and challenging spin: that wonderfulness is always available to us, ready to be found if only we learn to pay attention to it.

Recent findings suggest that easier mentioned than done, of course. Here, meditation and breathing exercises come to the fore as ways to build that attention muscle. This is where, 20 years ago, Carlson and Bailey, in their book Slowing Down to the Speed of Life, advocated doing things at half speed to help us take in the moment better. Something relatively easy to do and a good starting point. But learning to notice and see the wonderfulness of the now through our senses and a clarified mind is different, I believe, from proactively, more robustly creating it. Are we capable of doing that?

Yes, we can. Modern philosophers such as Hume, Nietzsche, and Kierkegaard, as well as ancients like Epicurus, advocated not dismissing logic but setting it aside, putting passion and desire on the front burner, and using them as a divining rod to guide our lives. But we can also combine them with mindfulness and the power of now: If we make present decisions based on our preferences, excitement, and passions, and support them with reason rather than impulse, we have a winning combination. We keep our ear close to ourselves, identify what we need, and act to create it, which in turn translates not only into a wonderful moment but ultimately into a wonderful life.

Industry observers note that so, are you ready to slow down, let the present seep more fully into your life, and pay attention? And maybe, taking a step further, actively practice making these moments the best they can be?

#184. As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the Stanford Center on Longevity rolled out in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions.
  • Another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging.
  • In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the Newly introduced Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the Stanford Center on Longevity rolled out in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that newly introduced and unprecedented reality.

Another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the Newly introduced Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

In a recent development, I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

According to recent reports, laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the Latest Map of Life. What are you seeing?

It has been revealed that LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

According to recent reports, already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act quickly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and noted, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”.

KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the Latest Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot promptly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering fresh products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

Sources indicate that KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

Sources indicate that it’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

It has been revealed that LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”.

While I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

We have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.
