How Psychological Flexibility Can Help Us Belong

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1446 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the key to belonging may be more within your reach than you think.
  • Psychological flexibility is your capacity to stay present, open to your inner experience, and engaged with what matters to you—even when things feel uncomfortable.
  • Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the key to belonging may be more within your reach than you think. You don’t need to become more interesting, more confident, or less awkward. You may simply need to become more psychologically flexible.

Psychological flexibility is your capacity to stay present, open to your inner experience, and engaged with what matters to you—even when things feel uncomfortable. Researchers have been studying this capacity for decades, and it turns out that when you are more psychologically flexible, you are not only less likely to struggle with anxiety and depression, you are also more capable of pursuing what matters to you. That might mean repairing  strained relationships, joining the exercise class you feel anxious about, or starting the book club you know would bring more conversation and connection into your life.

Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

It has been revealed that A recent study of more than 16,000 undergraduate students at 104 U.S. colleges and universities found that greater psychological flexibility was associated with a stronger sense of belonging. The study does not prove that flexibility causes belonging, but it points to something hopeful: Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

Emotional flexibility is your capacity to make room for the range of feelings that can come with being part of a group—whether you’re feeling left out, awkward, or nervous—without becoming overwhelmed by those emotions or needing to suppress them.

Meeting upcoming people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

According to recent reports, sometimes our emotions give us important information. Maybe you are dreading that work event because there’s heavy drinking, and it doesn’t align with your values. That discomfort may be worth listening to. At other times, feeling uncomfortable is simply part of the experience. Meeting latest people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

According to recent reports, try this small emotional flexibility practice: Imagine placing the feelings you’re having about a social situation into a backpack. How do you want to carry them? Do you want to shift the weight from side to side? Find someone to help you carry it? Or perhaps offer yourself some self compassion along the way? You may not get to decide what is inside the backpack, but you can decide how you carry it into your next interaction.

Every so often, look inside. Do these feelings have useful information for you? Do they  need care or attention? If not, adjust the straps and bring them along.

According to recent reports, your mind can be the world’s worst co-pilot when it comes to social situations. It compares you to others, judges you, makes negative predictions and sometimes is just plain mean.

Cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

Industry observers note that before entering a social event, write down some of the thoughts you’re having. Just noting a thought is a thought, helps you get some space from it. You get to decide if you want to take your mind’s advice, or just say thank you and move on.

Sources indicate that try this  cognitive defusion practice: When unhelpful thoughts return, try responding: “Thank you, mind. I know you are trying to help me. And I’ve decided to do this.”.

Industry observers note that the goal is not to get rid of the thoughts. It is to stop allowing them to make all your social decisions.

Industry observers note that when we feel as though we don’t belong, we often see ourselves through a narrow lens: I am not good at conversation. I am the only person who doesn’t know someone here. I never make a good first impression.

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like: I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who….

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like:.

I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who….

It has been revealed that these kinds of statements can make a passing experience feel like a permanent part of who we are. But pretty much everyone has felt socially awkward at one time or another, and nearly everyone longs to belong. And chances are, you aren’t always this way.

Try this self-flexibility practice: When you notice a  narrow view of yourself taking over, see whether you can become more flexible with your idea of “me.” Can you notice someone else who may be feeling similarly? Can you recognize a way that you are already connected—through your nervousness, or simply by sharing this moment? And can you see yourself as someone who isn’t defined by  “always” and “never”? What changes when you make room for sometimes instead?

Industry observers note that in ACT, values describe how you want to show up in your life. They are qualities of action— such as courageously, warmly, playfully, honestly, or presently.

Before entering a social situation, try this values practice. Ask yourself:.

How do I want to make others feel?

If I already felt like I fit in, how would I act?

It has been revealed that these questions help you identify how you want to participate and connect with others. You don’t have to wait until you feel confident or included. In fact, the more you act in alignment with your values, the more you may begin to experience yourself as someone who already belongs.

In a recent development, social anxiety has a way of pulling our attention inward. It shines a spotlight on how we look, whether we’re stumbling over our words, or what might go wrong next.

Try being more flexible with your attention. Notice your feet on the floor, listen to what the other person has to say, or take in the group as a whole. Shifting your focus like this can help you become less caught up in self-consciousness and more aware of what’s happening around you. There’s more to the scene than the words you are saying.

Sources indicate that try this attentional flexibility practice: When you notice yourself getting caught up in comparison or self-judgment, try shifting your attention. What are five things you see? What are four things you hear? What are three things you care about? What are two people you want to meet? What is one thing that matters most to you right now?

When you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way.

We build belonging one small connection at a time.

Sources indicate that when you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way. At the grocery store, strike up a conversation with the person grabbing lettuce next to you (“What salad are you making?”) At school pickup, get out of your car and wait with other caregivers (“Who’s your kid?”). If you are waiting for a yoga class to start, talk to the person next to you (“Have taken this class before?”) If  someone is sharing the space with you, you already have something in common. It takes courage to make that move, but small gestures like these can open the door to meaningful connections over time.

Use your other psychological flexibility skills to support you! Make room for discomfort, step back from unhelpful thoughts, shift your attention away from self-judgement, broaden your perspective,  and remember why you want to connect in the first place.

Sources indicate that psychological flexibility offers you a greater range of ways to respond, even when you feel like you don’t quite fit in. You can make room for anxiety, step back from your mind’s commentary, widen your sense of self, orient toward your values, return to the present, and make one small move toward connection.

Try out some of these skills, and you will notice, belonging is something you co-create, one flexible move at a time.

The backpack hits the floor, and "How was your day?" gets a one-word answer: "Fine." Kids don’t always say what’s on their mind, but a little time and attention may help them open up.

World Children’s Day is a good moment for parents, caregivers, and teachers to ask kids how they’re feeling and listen without trying to fix anything. The day honors children’s rights, including the right to be heard.

Here’s a look at what the day is about, plus a few activities that can help kids feel understood, at home or in the classroom.

Recent findings suggest that world Children's Day is a global day of action for children, run by UNICEF. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 20. This year’s theme is “My day. My rights. My future.” It invites children to tell world leaders what kind of future they want.

The day celebrates children and the rights they’re born with. In many places, children “take over” high-profile roles in media, sports, and government for the day. Landmarks light up blue to show support for children's rights.

November 20 marks two milestones for children’s rights. On this date in 1959, the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child, a statement of shared ideals. Thirty years later to the day, it adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989, a treaty that nations can commit to follow.

The Convention sets out the rights every child has, including the right to be safe, to play, and to have their opinions taken seriously. Nearly every country has formally agreed to follow it, and it’s the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history.

Countries around the world mark World Children’s Day. Many also celebrate a separate Children’s Day, most notably June 1, International Children's Day.

Some countries do pick dates of their own. Turkey celebrates on April 23, and India on November 14. The dates differ, but the idea is the same: it’s a day dedicated to the youngest members of a community.

In a recent development, you don’t need a significant event to mark World Children’s Day. A meta-analysis on children and teens linked understanding emotions with better social skills and fewer behavior problems. Kids can build that understanding in everyday moments, like the ones below.

It has been revealed that kids may not know they have rights, but those who learn about them may feel more confident speaking up. UNICEF’s child-friendly version of the Convention explains the rights in plain language.

Try: Read one or two rights together, then ask which feels most key to them.

Not every child has the words for how they feel. Invite them to sketch their day from morning to night, then have them walk you through it.

If they’re up for it, ask which part they loved most and which part felt hard. A drawing gives kids something concrete to point to as they talk, and that can feel easier than answering a broad question such as “How are you feeling?”.

Try: At home, pin the drawing to the fridge so your child can talk about it again if they’d like. In class, create an “Our Day” wall where kids can choose to share their drawings and spot the moments they had in common.

Recent findings suggest that when a child melts down, get curious about the feeling underneath. Help them put it into words: “It looks like you’re frustrated that it’s not your turn. Is that right?” Then listen carefully to their answer before you reassure them. “You’re fine” can sound dismissive, even when you mean well. When you talk about feelings this way, kids often learn to do it too.

Try: Post a chart of faces showing common feelings where kids can see it, and invite them to point to or say how they feel at the start of the day. Welcome any details they want to share.

💙 Once a big feeling has a name, here are coping skills for kids to try.

Industry observers note that set aside a few minutes at dinner or morning circle time for everyone to share one high, one low, and one thing they’re thankful for. Take a turn yourself so kids feel more at ease sharing.

Just listen as kids share, and try not to talk them out of a hard feeling. Kids tend to manage feelings better when you respond with warmth instead of brushing them off.

Try: Pass around a talking object, such as a small stuffed animal. Whoever holds it has the floor, grown-ups included.

💙 On Calm, listen to Feel Thankful With Thomas, a four-minute meditation for little ones, or the Gratitude session from the Classroom Mindfulness Tools series.

Industry observers note that A few minutes of meditation can be a soothing way for kids to slow down and settle. Sessions can focus on anything from breathing and body awareness to gratitude and kindness, so there’s room to follow your child’s interests or needs. Kids can sit, lie down, or stand, and they can stop whenever they’d like.

In a recent development, try: Belly breathing is a gentle place to start. Have your child lie down with a stuffed animal on their belly and watch it rise and fall as they breathe slowly.

Reading together gives you some time to connect, and stories can spark conversations about feelings. Kids may find it easier to talk about how a character feels than how they do.

Pick a book where a character is going through difficult feelings, then pause and ask, “What do you think she’s feeling?”.

In a recent development, try: At home, make the story the last part of your child’s bedtime routine to help them wind down. In class, read a few pages at the end of the day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A massive neuroimaging investigation involving 2,187 patients with multiple sclerosis reveals that grey matter atrophy does not accumulate at random; rather, it radiates outward from specific cortical and subcortical “disease epicenters.” Published by Mar Barrantes-Cepas and colleagues, the study provides strong clinical evidence for the “nodal stress hypothesis.”.

The authors demonstrate that high-degree topological network hubs, such as the visual, sensorimotor, and temporal cortices, alongside the thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala, are selectively vulnerable to neurodegenerative collapse because their intense metabolic demands exhaust local cells. The findings also document transneuronal degeneration propagating along structural connections, confirming that progressive neurodegeneration in multiple sclerosis occurs independently of acute inflammatory relapses.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) has long been defined as a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammatory demyelinating lesions scattered across the white matter of the central nervous system. Yet in recent decades, advanced neuroimaging has revealed an equally devastating, covert pathological hallmark: widespread, accelerated grey matter atrophy.

Unlike transient focal inflammation, grey matter volume loss begins during the earliest clinical stages, correlates directly with irreversible physical disability and cognitive decline, and progresses relentlessly even when disease-modifying therapies effectively suppress clinical relapses.

For years, the spatial patterning of this tissue loss remained elusive, presenting in non-random yet seemingly disparate cortical and subcortical distributions.

Now, in an extensive multicenter neuroimaging study evaluating MRI scans from 2,187 individuals diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a research team led by Mar Barrantes-Cepas and colleagues reveals the organizational logic behind this neurodegenerative spread.

Their work substantiates the nodal stress hypothesis, demonstrating that grey matter loss originates within high-traffic, hyper-connected “disease epicenters” and propagates throughout the connectome via transneuronal degeneration.

To map the spatiotemporal evolution of brain atrophy, the researchers utilized structural MRI datasets from an international cohort of 2,187 patients across various stages and clinical subtypes of multiple sclerosis, comparing localized tissue loss against normative connectome architecture.

The analysis revealed that the earliest and most severe tissue loss localized within the brain’s primary topological hubs. These “epicenters” included:.

Recent findings suggest that these findings provide large-scale empirical backing for the nodal stress hypothesis. In complex network topology, hubs represent the most critical communication centers, routing traffic across disparate functional modules.

It has been revealed that however, this central positioning carries a severe bioenergetic cost. High-degree hubs maintain higher baseline firing rates, express higher densities of energy-intensive ion channels, and require disproportionate mitochondrial ATP production to preserve synaptic transmission.

In multiple sclerosis, where chronic subclinical microglial inflammation, widespread demyelination, and oxidative stress compromise mitochondrial respiratory chain efficiency, these high-demand hubs become metabolic bottlenecks. The relentless functional demand exhausts cellular energy supplies, triggering localized axonal degeneration and neuronal apoptosis.

Sources indicate that the study demonstrated that once a disease epicenter begins to decay, the pathology does not remain confined. Instead, the scans revealed clear markers of transneuronal degeneration, a cascading process where damage in a primary hub travels anterogradely or retrogradely across anatomical white matter tracts to damage downstream connected neurons.

As high-traffic epicenters fail, their connected secondary and tertiary structural partners lose vital neurotrophic support and experience excitotoxic or disuse stress, causing neurodegeneration to systematically ripple through the structural connectome.

Crucially, the investigators tracked how these network-based degradation pathways differed across relapsing-remitting and progressive forms of the disease, finding that network-level strain drives disability accumulation across all cohorts.

Recent findings suggest that “It is now clear that disease progression can occur independently of relapses and acute inflammation,” write Barrantes-Cepas and colleagues. “Network-based measures, which are easily obtainable from conventional MRI and normative datasets, could be used to explain future atrophy progression in individual patients.”.

The recognition that multiple sclerosis progression is driven by network-mediated metabolic exhaustion challenges the classical clinical focus on managing only acute, gadolinium-enhancing white matter lesions.

Industry observers note that because conventional MRI scans routinely collected in routine clinical practice can be evaluated using normative connectome templates, network-based nodal stress modeling offers a low-cost, non-invasive prognostic tool. Clinicians could potentially map an individual’s specific epicenter vulnerability early in the disease course, forecasting spatial trajectories of grey matter loss years before clinical deficits emerge.

Furthermore, these findings highlight fresh avenues for neuroprotective drug discovery: therapies designed to bolster mitochondrial bioenergetics, protect against metabolic exhaustion, or buffer high-traffic hubs from metabolic overload could provide the missing therapeutic weapon needed to halt progressive disability in multiple sclerosis.

How does grey matter atrophy spread through the brain in multiple sclerosis?

Atrophy does not spread at random. It originates in specific “disease epicenters”, the brain’s most heavily connected topological hubs, such as the thalamus, hippocampus, visual, and sensorimotor cortices. From these epicenters, damage propagates to distant brain regions along structural nerve pathways through transneuronal degeneration.

What is the “nodal stress hypothesis”?

The nodal stress hypothesis suggests that brain hubs with the highest number of connections are under constant, intense metabolic strain because they must process and route massive amounts of neural communication. In multiple sclerosis, where energy production is already impaired, these high-traffic hubs suffer metabolic exhaustion, making them the first to degenerate.

Can multiple sclerosis worsen without relapses or acute inflammation?

Yes. This study confirms that progressive neurodegeneration and brain volume loss can proceed independently of acute clinical relapses and active autoimmune lesions, driven instead by chronic network-based metabolic failure and structural disconnectivity.

The role of network connectivity and transcriptomic vulnerability in shaping gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis.

Industry observers note that clinical progression is strongly linked to gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis (MS), detectable early on MRI and progressing nonrandomly across the brain. However, the mechanisms driving its spatiotemporal progression and individual variability remain unclear.

In a recent development, using MRIs from 2187 participants, alongside normative data, we systematically investigated network-based mechanisms underlying MS-related atrophy. Regional atrophy was associated with functional cortical hubness, supporting the nodal stress hypothesis, and was constrained by anatomical and functional connections, consistent with transneuronal degeneration. Lesional disconnection and transcriptomic vulnerability played marginal roles.

Sources indicate that patient- and subgroup-level analyses revealed that network-based mechanisms are specifically linked to MS-related neurodegeneration and may operate differently in distinct subtypes or disease phases. Atrophy patterns were anchored to the connectivity profiles of disease epicenters involving the visual, sensorimotor, and temporal cortices, as well as the hippocampi, amygdalae, and thalami.

Network-based measures enhanced the explanation of future atrophy progression in people with MS, providing a mechanistic framework to understand neurodegeneration in MS.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in our recent On Being conversation, NASA astrophysicist and exoplanet researcher Natalie Batalha said something that stopped me up short: as sentient beings endowed with awareness, we are “the universe itself becoming aware.” Echoing poet Diane Ackerman’s lovely notion of “the plain everythingness of everything, in cahoots with the everythingness of everything else,” Dr. Batalha added: “It took 13.7 billion years for the atoms to come together to create the portal to the universe which is my physical self. So in that statement is this idea, or the fluidity of time and space. And I kind of see it all at once. And I don’t know what ‘me’ is. I just feel part of everything. And I feel such deep gratitude for being able to take this conscious look at the universe — at myself as being part of the universe.”.

The sentiment reminded me of a beautiful interview Carl Sagan (November 9, 1934–December 20, 1996) gave shortly after the premiere of his epoch-making documentary Cosmos, later included in Conversations with Carl Sagan (public library).

In late August of 1980 — two years after he conducted Susan Sontag’s most dimensional interview and nine years before his magnificent conversation with Leonard Bernstein — interlocutor extraordinaire Jonathan Cott visited Sagan’s home in Los Angeles to interview him for Rolling Stone. In the soaring the conversation that followed, Sagan stepped into his native nexus of the scientific and the poetic to contemplate our understanding of the universe and of ourselves, the nature of reality and of human knowledge, and how to live with the unknown.

In a recent development, it’s a critical moment in the history of the world… We are the representatives of the cosmos; we are an example of what hydrogen atoms can do, given fifteen billion years of cosmic evolution. And we resonate to these questions. We start with the origin of every human being, and then the origin of our community, our nation, the human species, who our ancestors were and then the riddle of the origin of life. And the questions: where did the Earth and Solar System come from? Where did the galaxies come from?

Recent findings suggest that every one of those questions is deep and significant. They are the subject of folklore, myth, superstition, and religion in every human culture. But for the first time we are on the verge of answering many of them. I don’t mean to suggest that we have the final answers; we are bathing in mystery and confusion on many subjects, and I think that will always be our destiny. The universe will always be much richer than our ability to understand it.

Recent findings suggest that to be sure, understanding the whole of the universe seems like too grandiose an aspiration when we are continually struggling to understand the tiny subset of the universe that is ourselves. Three summers before this interview, Sagan had spearheaded The Golden Record — a poetic attempt at such self-comprehension, mirroring humanity back to itself. Now, with an eye to another landmark triumph of self-reflection made possible by scientific progress — the iconic Earthrise photograph taken by the astronauts of Apollo 8 in 1968 — Sagan considers the immense and paradoxical gift of cosmic perspective:.

Recent findings suggest that you saw [Earth] for the first time as a tiny blue ball floating in space. You realized that there were other, similar worlds far away, of different size, different color and constitution. You got the idea that our planet was just one in a multitude. I think there are two apparently contradictory and still very powerful benefits of that cosmic perspective — the sense of our planet as one in a vast number and the sense of our planet as a place whose destiny depends upon us.

It has been revealed that in this awareness resides a humbling and disquieting reminder of our creaturely limitations. We navigate the world by our common-sense perception, but that perception has blinded us to reality again and again. We have mistaken our sensorial intuitions for facts of the universe — for millennia, we held wrong beliefs about Earth’s shape, motion, and position, because it feels flat and static beneath our feet, and central to the order of the cosmos. We have mistrusted processes and phenomena beyond the boundaries of what we can touch and feel with our limited senses — from evolution, which unfolds on scales of time too vast to be visible within a human lifetime, to quantum mechanics, which operates on subatomic scales imperceptible and almost inconceivable to the human observer. Long before Sagan equipped us with an antidote to the “common pitfalls of common sense” in his timeless Baloney Detection Kit for critical thinking, he tells Cott:.

Recent findings suggest that common sense works fine for the universe we’re used to, for time scales of decades, for a space between a tenth of a millimeter and a few thousand kilometers, and for speeds much less than the speed of light. Once we leave those domains of human experience, there’s no reason to expect the laws of nature to continue to obey our expectations, since our expectations are dependent on a limited set of experiences.

We have to be very careful not to impose our hopes and desires on the cosmos, but instead, in the scientific tradition and with the most open mind possible, see what the cosmos is saying to us.

Sagan points to one particularly blatant obfuscation of reality driven by our self-centered hopes, desires, and delusions — astrology:.

[Astrology is] like racism or sexism: you have twelve little pigeonholes, and as soon as you type someone as a member of that particular group, as long as someone is an Aquarius, Virgo or Scorpio, you know his characteristics. It saves you the effort of getting to know him individually.

According to recent reports, sagan ends by considering the nature of human knowledge itself. Drawing on its past, he projects its future:.

Human knowledge is a set of successive approximations… There are all sorts of things that we’ve gotten wrong, and all sorts of mind-boggling things that we can’t even glimpse that will be the established fact in a century or two.

Recent findings suggest that there are two extremes to worry about. One is the extreme in which everything is known and there’s nothing left to do. The other is where everything is so complicated you can never begin to do anything. We are lucky to live in a universe were there are laws of nature and things to discover, but they’re not impossibly difficult, so we can understand them to some extent. But they’re also difficult enough so that we’re nowhere near understanding them all. There are exhilarating discoveries yet to be made. It’s the best possible world.

Complement with Diane Ackerman — a favorite poet of Sagan’s, who was her doctoral advisor — on our longing to know the universe beyond ourselves and Primo Levi on the spiritual value of space exploration, then revisit Sagan on the value of uncertainty, the enchantment of chemistry, and the most crucial perspective in the human world.

Tech Report: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner.
  • Sources indicate that remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives.
  • This ability tends to weaken as we grow older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface.

Sources indicate that remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car.

This ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that A newly introduced study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers important clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight.

"This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," mentioned Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science.

The research was published in Nature Neuroscience.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Store Memories.

Recent findings suggest that sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially crucial for maintaining healthy brain function.

During this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex.

"Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon said. "Our study indicates that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep.".

The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Disrupted Brain Waves.

To investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s.

The differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups.

The team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances.

The scans revealed that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep.

Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease.

"These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon said. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age.".

Sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age.

Mysterious "Lonely Waves" Linked to Memory Loss.

The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information.

To test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight.

Sources indicate that participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves.".

Industry observers note that the team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined.

It has been revealed that these observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible.

Additional Tests Strengthen the Connection.

Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity.

Industry observers note that they collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging.

It has been revealed that unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction.

People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid.

The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings.

"It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon said.

Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep.

"This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon noted.

What Deep Sleep Reveals About the Aging Brain.

Although memory often declines with age, the fresh research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories.

Recent findings suggest that "It's not just about age," Sharon remarked. "It's how much pathology you have in frontal areas where global waves originate.".

In a recent development, sleep quality also appears to be part of the picture. Although it can be difficult to define or measure precisely, the organization and movement of slow brain waves may provide crucial indicators of how effectively the brain performs its nighttime memory functions.

According to recent reports, the findings raise the possibility that changes in deep sleep activity could eventually help researchers better understand or identify early memory problems. They also point toward potential targets for future treatments aimed at protecting memory as people age.

In a recent development, for now, however, a central question remains unanswered. Scientists still need to determine whether accumulating tau contributes to the breakdown of synchronized sleep waves, whether changes in those waves influence tau accumulation, or whether the relationship involves additional processes.

Recent findings suggest that "We can see tau and lonely waves rising together over time," Sharon said. "What we cannot yet say is which leads -- and that question will shape how we design interventions.".

It has been revealed that the study's additional co-authors include Xi Chen, James Westphal, Chelsea Brown, and Vyoma D. Shah of UC Berkeley, along with Jason Dude of Washington University in St. Louis.

Funding came from grants awarded by the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health. Sharon also received support through a Glenn Foundation for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship and a Weill Neurohub Fellowship.

Here are some patterns to observe to discern whether your child’s stomach pain is associated with anxiety or an underlying medical condition.

Sources indicate that Q: “My child has anxiety and often complains of tummy aches. How do I know if the stomachaches are related to anxiety or a medical condition? How do I know when to see a doctor?”.

In a recent development, as parents, it’s tricky to untangle common complaints about stomachaches from chronic anxiety, an underlying medical problem, or even school avoidance. Here are a few ways to tell the difference, and clear signs that it’s time to seek medical help.

Understand the mind-body connection. Our gut and brain are in constant conversation. When a child feels overwhelmed, scared, or worried, their body will respond with stomach pain, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, and a generalized discomfort. These symptoms are not imagined or exaggerated; they are physical reactions to emotional stress.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

Industry observers note that observe timing and patterns. When are stomachaches happening? Stomach pain related to anxiety trends to show up during specific times: before and around school, tests, social events, and bedtime. Does your child’s stomachache dissipate after these types of events, or when they are comforted or distracted?

Are your child’s stomach pains taking place at night? Are they making it difficult for your child to eat? Are they losing weight? Is your child experiencing chronic diarrhea or do they have blood in their stool? Are they vomiting? These symptoms are more indicative of an underlying medical condition, especially if they become worse over time.

Keep a log. Track when your child has stomach pains to help you discern whether it’s due to anxiety or an underlying medical condition. Occasional stomachaches that happen during stressful times are common.

However, if your child complains of a stomachache several times each week for more than a month, consult with your pediatrician or seek a gastroenterologist.

[Read: “5 Ways to Reframe Anxiety for Your Worried Teen”].

According to recent reports, and remember: You don’t have to choose between taking anxiety seriously and taking physical symptoms seriously. Both deserve attention. By watching for patterns, listening carefully, and seeking help when needed, you’re doing exactly what your child needs: letting them know that any pain they experience matters.

#61. Why Nervous System Hyperarousal Keeps Jolting You Awake

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1333 w)

Why Nervous System Hyperarousal Keeps Jolting You Awake

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A psychological and sleep research study published in PLOS Mental Health reveals that people who frequently startle awake while drifting off to sleep, a phenomenon known as “sleep starts” or hypnic jerks, report significantly poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, and heightened anxiety.
  • Sources indicate that conducted by Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus at Paris Lodron University Salzburg, the investigation examined 194 adults across Austria and Germany.
  • Recent findings suggest that just as consciousness begins to dissolve and the body relaxes into slumber, an abrupt, violent jolt shatters the transition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A psychological and sleep research study published in PLOS Mental Health reveals that people who frequently startle awake while drifting off to sleep, a phenomenon known as “sleep starts” or hypnic jerks, report significantly poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, and heightened anxiety.

Sources indicate that conducted by Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus at Paris Lodron University Salzburg, the investigation examined 194 adults across Austria and Germany. The researchers discovered that frequent sleep starts do not merely represent isolated motor twitches, but manifest alongside autonomic surges, sensory flashes, and cognitive-emotional hyperarousal driven by unhelpful beliefs and acute pressure to fall asleep.

Recent findings suggest that just as consciousness begins to dissolve and the body relaxes into slumber, an abrupt, violent jolt shatters the transition. Often accompanied by the vivid sensation of tumbling into an abyss, an electric zap down the spine, or a blinding flash of light, the heart races as the sleeper gasps awake in sudden panic.

Known medically as “sleep starts” or hypnic jerks, these sudden myoclonic twitches occur at the boundary between wakefulness and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. While sporadic sleep starts are a benign, universal human experience, for a substantial subset of the population they recur persistently, transforming the threshold of sleep into a source of dread.

In a study published in the open-access journal PLOS Mental Health, researchers Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of the Centre for Cognitive Neuroscience at Paris Lodron University Salzburg, Austria, investigated the psychological and physiological profile of individuals afflicted by chronic hypnic jerks.

Their findings indicate that recurrent sleep starts are not isolated neuromuscular glitches; rather, they serve as a behavioral manifestation of sleep-related hyperarousal and cognitive-emotional anxiety.

Because standardized psychometric tools for quantifying hypnic jerks have historically been lacking, the research team synthesized existing clinical neurology and sleep medicine literature to construct a targeted assessment battery.

They surveyed 194 adults across Austria and Germany, dividing them into two cohorts: 96 individuals who experienced abrupt awakenings accompanied by at least one secondary symptom weekly, and 98 matched control participants without frequent sleep starts. Participants completed validated measures assessing insomnia severity, subjective sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, dysfunctional beliefs about sleep, anxiety, and depression.

The resulting symptom profiles revealed that sleep starts involve a multi-sensory and autonomic cascade:.

Recent findings suggest that “Sleep starts are much more than a simple muscle twitch when falling asleep,” explains first author Tanja Grünberger. “Participants described not only jerks, but also sensations of falling, a racing heart, flashes of light or loud bangs, and strong feelings of alarm or fear – and those who reported sleep starts at least once a week also reported poorer sleep quality, more unhelpful beliefs about sleep and more anxiety symptoms.”.

Recent findings suggest that when comparing the two cohorts, the differences were statistically pronounced. Individuals experiencing weekly sleep starts had significantly poorer overall sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, higher levels of general anxiety, elevated depressive symptoms, and more dysfunctional beliefs regarding sleep.

According to recent reports, statistical modeling revealed that how frequently people experienced sleep starts was closely tied to sleep quality, rigid sleep beliefs, and anxiety levels. Together with demographic variables (age and gender), these psychological factors accounted for 26.9% of the variance in sleep start frequency between individuals.

Importantly, participants reported that sleep starts surged during periods of psychological distress and emotional strain. In contrast, physical sleep deprivation was less influential on the frequency of episodes.

“What we found most interesting was how closely sleep starts are linked to how people think and feel about sleep,” Grünberger notes. “The more strongly participants held unhelpful beliefs about sleep and the more anxious they were, the more often they reported sleep starts – and in the moment itself, many described a strong pressure to finally fall asleep. Our data cannot show what causes what, but this pattern resembles what we know from insomnia.”.

Sources indicate that traditional medical advice has often dismissed hypnic jerks as inconsequential physiological quirks requiring no clinical management. However, the Salzburg findings show that for individuals caught in chronic hyperarousal, sleep starts create a self-reinforcing loop: pre-sleep anxiety increases nervous system excitability, triggering a violent startle response, which then reinforces catastrophic beliefs about one’s inability to sleep.

“These findings support the view that sleep starts should be considered within broader frameworks of sleep-related hyperarousal and cognitive-emotional activation,” the authors write.

Industry observers note that looking forward, senior author Manuel Schabus highlights the therapeutic avenues this connection opens: “For most people, sleep starts are a harmless feature of falling asleep. For a subgroup, however, they go along with distress and a longer time to fall asleep. Whether approaches that reduce arousal and sleep-related worry also help with distressing sleep starts has not yet been tested – that is an important next step.”.

Targeted cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), autonomic down-regulation protocols, and pre-sleep relaxation techniques could offer relief for patients whose transition into slumber is repeatedly derailed by their own nervous system.

What are sleep starts or hypnic jerks?

Industry observers note that sleep starts are sudden, involuntary muscle twitches or jolts that occur during the transition from wakefulness to sleep. They can be strong enough to wake a person fully and are often accompanied by sensations of falling, electric shocks, flashes of light, a racing heart, and a sudden surge of fear or alarm.

How do frequent sleep starts relate to mental health and sleep disorders?

People who experience sleep starts at least weekly report significantly worse sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, higher anxiety, and more dysfunctional beliefs about sleep compared to those who do not. The frequency of these jolts tracks closely with daytime emotional strain and psychological stress.

What causes sleep starts to happen more often?

In a recent development, while occasional jerks are normal, frequent episodes appear driven by central nervous system hyperarousal. Heightened stress, performance anxiety around falling asleep, and catastrophic beliefs about insomnia keep the autonomic nervous system on high alert, triggering a startle response instead of a smooth physiological descent into sleep.

Phenomenology and associations with sleep, psychological, and demographic characteristics.

Sleep starts (SS) are transient phenomena during sleep onset. Although traditionally characterized by sudden muscle jerks, they may also involve sensory, cognitive, emotional, and autonomic experiences. Despite their high prevalence, empirical data on phenomenology and associated characteristics remain limited. This online survey examined SS phenomenology and exploratory associations with demographic, sleep-related, and psychological variables in 194 adults.

According to recent reports, participants with self-reported sleep-related movement disorders or relevant medical conditions were excluded. Individuals reporting abrupt awakenings ≥1/week and ≥1 additional symptom formed the SS group (SS frequency ≥1, n = 96); all others the comparison group (SS frequency <1, n = 98). Because SS were operationalized using self-reported symptoms, they could not be distinguished from related sleep-onset phenomena (e.g., exploding head syndrome, hypnagogic hallucinations).

It has been revealed that standardized questionnaires (PSQI, ISI, ESS, MZS, HADS) assessed sleep quality, insomnia severity, daytime sleepiness, dysfunctional sleep-related beliefs, and anxiety/depression symptoms. Participants described diverse experiences including motor jerks, falling sensations, dream-like experiences, somatosensory symptoms, autonomic arousal, and emotional reactions, accompanied by alarm, anxiety, and confusion.

Compared with controls, the SS group reported poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, stronger dysfunctional sleep-related beliefs, and higher anxiety/depressive symptoms (all p < .05). Exploratory regression analyses indicated that poorer sleep quality, stronger dysfunctional sleep-related beliefs, and higher anxiety symptoms were associated with higher SS frequency, whereas depressive symptoms were not. The final model explained 26.9% of variance (R2 = .269, adjusted R2 = .245).

It has been revealed that more frequent SS were retrospectively reported during emotional stress, whereas sleep deprivation was perceived as less influential. Although many described SS as manageable, a substantial subgroup reported distress and sleep disruption.

Sources indicate that this suggests that SS represent heterogeneous sleep-onset experiences associated with subjective sleep disturbance and cognitive-emotional arousal. Although causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional self-report data, the results highlight potentially relevant links between SS and sleep-related cognitive-emotional processes.

#60. Harness Neuroscience to Improve Psychological First Aid

Harness Neuroscience to Improve Psychological First Aid

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Sources indicate that psychological first aid (PFA) may be the first and most effective of psychological crisis interventions.
  • Sources indicate that menon's (2011) Triple Network Model proposes that three large-scale brain networks serve as the underlying neural circuits for attention and cognitive appraisal, emotion, and reactive adaptive behavior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Sources indicate that psychological first aid (PFA) may be the first and most effective of psychological crisis interventions. Recommended by the World Health Organization, the United Nations, the American Red Cross, and the American Psychological Association, it is not only being applied in disaster settings but is also being used to expand psychological support in communities in non-disaster situations. While research has demonstrated that PFA can be effective, training in how to apply PFA would seem essential. A recent study by Watanabe and others (Watanabe et al., 2026) on the neuroscience of the resilient brain may improve the efficiency of PFA by identifying the brain regions PFA should target.

Sources indicate that menon's (2011) Triple Network Model proposes that three large-scale brain networks serve as the underlying neural circuits for attention and cognitive appraisal, emotion, and reactive adaptive behavior. Dysregulation of these networks is believed to be the neurological underpinning of low resilience and distress during and in the wake of crisis. Conversely, highly integrated and complementary functioning within these same areas appears to be the neurological underpinning of resilience and adaptive functioning.

The Triple Network consists of the salience network (SN), the default mode network (DMN), and the executive control network (ECN). The SN prioritizes incoming information, assesses importance, detects threats, directs attention, and mobilizes defense mechanisms. It answers the question “What happened and what’s really crucial in this moment?” The DMN is the neural foundation for self-reflection, retrospection, introspection, and making meaning out of experiences. It is also involved in social connection. The DMN answers the question, “What does this mean to me?” The ECN engages working memory for planning, problem-solving, and goal-directed behavior. This network allows individuals to exert top-down cognitive control over emotion and implement effective coping strategies. The ECN answers the question, “How should I react?” Based on the determination of the DMN, the ECN can then also answer the question, ”Is there another way of interpreting this?” The ECN and DMN collaborate for problem-solving, cognitive reappraisal, and fostering adaptive coping.

Research has found that resilient individuals show increased activity and interaction between the DMN and the ECN with diminished activity in the SN. Less resilient individuals show increased and prolonged activity in the SN.

The work of Menon may provide a working heuristic as a foundation for practical application. So, perhaps the effectiveness of PFA can be enhanced by using interventions that target the resilience mechanisms residing in the DMN and the ECN while dampening the SN. More specifically, the neuroimaging literature on resilience suggests that PFA might be used to induce, externally, the same functional brain state that resilient individuals appear to achieve internally.

It has been revealed that when assisting a person in crisis, numerous sources have proposed that asking questions may be more effective than providing immediate answers (Everly & Lating, 2026). A simple set of questions targeting Menon’s Triple Network may help improve the efficiency and perhaps the effectiveness of PFA:.

The research also suggests the window for promoting resilience may come after 60 minutes or more, as the SN takes physiological priority in the first hour.

While intuition would suggest solving the immediate problem is always the best crisis intervention, that may not be true in all cases. The notion of using questions to catalyze reflection and introspection (DMN) and foster reappraisal (ECN) is not new. Socrates, often considered the greatest teacher of his time, embraced the question rather than the answer as a means of teaching and empowering. Perhaps that is a lesson we all can learn as we endeavor to assist others in distress.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Humans are constantly reinventing ways to maintain intimacy with the people we care about most. Today, one of our most ubiquitous connection rituals is reel sharing—that is, sending short social media videos to each other. At a time when much of the conversation about technology centers on how it is eroding human connection, reel sharing and the unspoken social norms that surround it suggest another possibility: a tool to maintain social bonds.

It has been revealed that this has been my experience. I met my best friend of more than 25 years, Kyra, when I was a Peace Corps volunteer. Our friendship formed before social media and with geographic distance between us (she served in Togo and I was in Cameroon). During Peace Corps service, we mainly stayed in touch through sporadic emails. After Peace Corps, we both started careers in international development, got married, and had a few kids. Our geographic separation didn’t change, but our time to email and chat on the phone did, significantly limiting our communication. I missed her.

Industry observers note that A couple of years ago, we started sending each other reels through Facebook (her preference) and Instagram (my preference). It became our version of “I’m thinking of you” or “Here’s something to brighten your day”—an asynchronous way of staying connected, sharing our interests, and quietly checking our emotional attunement with one another. Sending reels has helped to strengthen our friendship at a cadence that works for our busy lives.

According to recent reports, but there’s a tension with this practice, which is the guilt I sometimes feel about spending so much time on social media. Though an estimated 37–71% of Americans use social media sites, many have turned against them altogether, inviting us to throw out both the baby and the bathwater. Indeed, the parent organization of Facebook and Instagram (Meta) recently settled a lawsuit (for billions of dollars) that alleged that their sites were intentionally designed to addict children and teens.

Industry observers note that there might be good reasons to restrain social media use, but people will continue to use it—and so the question becomes: How can they use it wisely? Perhaps repositioning social media reel sending as a ritual of connection can help to recalibrate how and why we engage with the platform.

Recent findings suggest that social science sees interpersonal rituals as repetitive, symbolic actions that foster belonging and communicate shared meaning. Such rituals are routinized actions or behaviors that have unspoken norms understood by the participants. Performing the ritual with others symbolizes their importance in our lives and creates an opportunity for shared meaning, which collectively reinforces the bond.

Recent findings suggest that sending reels has become a modernized form of relationship maintenance, done to keep a relationship alive, relevant, and emotionally present. Relationship maintenance is a behavior we engage in to show our commitment to a relationship. There are both routine and strategic forms of relationship maintenance. We employ these tactics across all types of relationships: romantic, platonic, familial, and professional.

Routine maintenance consist of frequent, intuitive acts done to stay connected to the person through regular communication and information sharing—as opposed to grander gestures like buying flowers and other gifts, showing up at difficult moments, or bringing someone to the airport.

Industry observers note that the reason we feel irritated when our reel sending doesn’t receive a reaction is because relationships are rooted in social exchange. Essentially, relationships are based on a subconscious cost-benefit analysis, where reciprocity is expected, although not explicitly stated. Behaviors that are rewarded will continue—but the absence of reward can harm the relationship.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps you’re a mom who recently started sending reels to your adult daughter to reinforce regular communication. You’ll likely continue to do so until you realize, “Wait, she hasn’t responded.” While the action of sending reels is something we may do without much thought, we expect acknowledgment of the gesture: a like, emoji, comment, or reciprocal sending. When we don’t receive that, we feel disappointed. But when we do get the anticipated response, we feel closer to the person.

Sources indicate that kyra and I use a combination of emojis and reciprocal sending to signify reception. We’re so committed to reciprocal sending, that the other day she sent me this reel to remind me what to do if a couple of days went by without her sending me anything!

According to recent reports, think about the last person you sent a reel to. Who was it? I’m willing to bet they were a close friend, relative, or romantic partner. That’s because reels are typically shared with someone you care about, someone you want to be in community with, and the goal is to reinforce closeness.

While research focused on sending reels as a form of digital communication is scarce, we can extrapolate the link between relationship closeness and reel-sending behavior from studies focused on digital memes (static photos) and GIFs (looping animations).

Researchers asked 395 study participants, ranging in age from 18 to 75, to recall situations where they sent a text message to a strong tie (close relationship) and a weak tie (acquaintance) and report their use of graphic icons such as memes, GIFs, and emojis. Participants reported more sharing with strong ties than weak ties.

Those who used graphic icons more frequently reported greater feelings of self-disclosure (“I can talk to X about anything”), relationship maintenance (We “try to make each other laugh”), and intimacy (“How often do you tell your friend everything that you are going through?”).

Admittedly, sending a reel to someone requires a bit of vulnerability.

You are taking a risk by sending something that resonates with you, but you aren’t 100% sure will resonate and be reciprocated by the other person. The likelihood of success depends on how accurately you guessed the person’s likes or dislikes.

The vulnerability factor is another reason we are more likely to send reels to close others; vulnerability typically follows closeness, not the other way around. When we are vulnerable with people we are close to, the risk is diminished because we know them better. If it fails, the potential harm is cushioned by our established relationship.

Recent findings suggest that aside from the vulnerability factor, there’s a reason when you’re scrolling social media that you don’t see a reel and immediately think to send it to Bob in accounting or your dentist. While they may be cool people, they simply aren’t top of mind for you.

Close relationships carry emotional weight, and our brain is much more likely to remember emotionally salient information. For example, Kyra has three very active sons who all play competitive sports. Her weekends are consumed with sporting events, so every time I see a post about sports moms, I think of her and send it. It’s my way of recognizing her efforts and sacrifice.

In a recent development, reels are digital objects that can trigger us to think of others. Because we have much more information about close relationships and cognitively our experiences with them are more accessible, when we want to share a reel, we pick from this list of people.

Shared experiences are an vital component of fostering connections, serving as the foundation for establishing shared meaning. When you’re in the same physical space, this might look like watching movies together, attending events, or sharing meals.

Reels offer an asynchronous substitute for shared experiences. By viewing a reel, and maybe even sharing a brief commentary on it, and then sending it to a connection who then reacts, you are creating a digital shared experience—viewing and reacting to the same content.

Shared experiences help us to understand the preferences and thoughts of others, while sharing our own. Through this exchange, we can align our minds and create shared meaning. It’s a form of emotional attunement, a core component of close social connection.

Sources indicate that sending reels tests out that alignment. Essentially, when we send reels, we are saying, “I found this to be funny, did you?” or “This really resonated with me, how about you?”  or “I thought this information would be useful to you, is it?” The validation of alignment is in the receiver’s reaction.

When distance or busyness prevent or limit in-person interaction, sending reels allows us to share funny, thought-provoking, or motivational content with people we care about, maintaining a sense of closeness, having laughed, gasped, or become angry at the same reel. We reinforce connection through mutual understanding and shared meaning.

If you send reels and you’ve categorized it as a “guilty pleasure,” I’d encourage you to reconsider the guilt part. Guilt suggests you are doing something bad when the intention and the value behind sending the reel is likely anything but.

The all-or-nothing culture of social media today doesn’t give space for a more nuanced look at our productive use of these platforms and overlooks that some of our online engagement reflects values-based behaviors.

The question is not simply how much time we spend on social media, but what we are doing there. Compulsive scrolling and intentionally connecting with someone we care about may occur on the same platform, but they are not the same.

Sources indicate that so, keep sending the reels, not as the only sign that you care, but as one of many in your interpersonal toolbox. I know Kyra and I don’t initiative on stopping anytime soon!

What Makes You Yourself: Posidonia Australis, Pando, and the Paradox of Personhood

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, an organism is a mortal unit of matter distinct from other organisms by its genome — the possibilities encoded in its particular genetic makeup — and its phenotype — the set of traits expressed, the actualities summoned by adaptation and chance from its possibilities.
  • It has been revealed that humans are the only animals, save perhaps the bowerbird, who can alter their phenotype by means of their own making — grow, cut, and dye their hair, tattoo and tan their skin, increase and decrease the size of various body parts with scalpel and silicone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, bigger than Manhattan, Earth’s largest living organism sways in the surf south of Australia: Posidonia australis — a species of seagrass that, unable to flower, clones itself. Older than mathematics and the written word, it has been cloning itself since before the pyramids were built — a kind of immortality. And while I kiss my lover on the fresh-cut grass under the Manhattan Bridge, it goes on cloning itself as we go on dying and passing between our lips the heat of our mortality.

In a recent development, an organism is a mortal unit of matter distinct from other organisms by its genome — the possibilities encoded in its particular genetic makeup — and its phenotype — the set of traits expressed, the actualities summoned by adaptation and chance from its possibilities. Human beings are organisms encased in the hardest yet most vulnerable exoskeleton in nature: a self. A self includes but surpasses the organism to encompass its environment and its social context, the psychological terrain of memory and desire, the fingerprints left on it by the touch of other selves. An organism ends at the physical boundary of its body, but a self does not — we spend our lives negotiating where we end and the world begins.

It has been revealed that humans are the only animals, save perhaps the bowerbird, who can alter their phenotype by means of their own making — grow, cut, and dye their hair, tattoo and tan their skin, increase and decrease the size of various body parts with scalpel and silicone. We are also the only animal who can radically alter both its environment and its social context, building elaborate homes on faraway landmasses, reconstituting our families and friend groups, changing the labors by which we put food on our table. Our selves are not like our cells, replacing themselves with clones in the course of living, but like Russian nesting dolls, each prior self outgrown but contained by the next. (“We are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not,” Joan Didion wrote.) Our lives a relay race, running from the selves we have outgrown or wish to outgrow towards the selves we try to become to or are unconsciously becoming, the baton of personhood passed from one to the next along the arrow of time, the track of our mortality.

Sources indicate that this puts us in a peculiar predicament: Each human lifetime is lived by a single organism that contains a multitude of selves, genetically continuous and psychologically discontinuous, making it impossible to define where and what the person is. What, then, makes you yourself across all those replaced cells and reconfigured selves?

Organisms like Posidonia australis, which both conceal and reveal the nature of the self, may give us the best hint at an answer — one which evolutionary biologist Rowan Hooper articulates beautifully in his book Togetherness: Symbiosis and the Hidden Story of Life’s Greatest Collaborations (public library). Considering Earth’s largest living tree, he writes:.

Recent findings suggest that the Pando aspen grove in Utah comprises 47,000 trees, all genetically identical, connected by a vast root system. Language immediately becomes limiting when trying to describe Pando. Do we call the forest an organism? An entity? It has been estimated to weigh nearly 6 million kilograms, or 6,000 tonnes. If it helps, that’s about thirty-five blue whales or 1,000 elephants. It is one of the oldest organisms on Earth. Its cells are living and dying over time, but the DNA remains pretty much unchanged. That is, the entity lives on, even as its parts die.

With an eye to the Ship of Theseus — Plutarch’s timeless thought experiment about the nature of the self — he reflects:.

Pando is biology’s Ship of Theseus — is it the same tree as when it first sprouted? I think not. It’s more like a continuation of the idea of Pando… The 47,000 stems of Pando start off genetically the same, but grow phenotypically different; a forest, but also a mass of individuals.

Industry observers note that “The word for world is forest,” Ursula K. Le Guin wrote in her subtle insistence that symbiosis — the ultimate unselfing of the organism — is what made this rocky planet a living world. Rustling through the canopy of the Pando is the whisper of an answer to the unnerving question of what makes a body a person: You are not your roots, not the stem of your circumstance, not your branching choices. You are the idea of you, the forest of your selves in constant conviviality with other selves, called again and again to unself into who you really are.

#56. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (893 w)
