The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but fresh research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe.
  • For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences.
  • In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but fresh research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD.".

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear.

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

Sources indicate that the researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," remarked Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger.

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

In a recent development, "The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters.".

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD.

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

It has been revealed that for someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

Sources indicate that "Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'.".

According to recent reports, because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a newly introduced way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

#55. Industry News: Brain Moves Its Touch Center to Keep Feeling Sensation

Industry News: Brain Moves Its Touch Center to Keep Feeling Sensation

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that biomedical engineers at Penn State have solved a major hurdle in neuroprosthetics and sensory rehabilitation: sensory habituation, where the brain gradually stops perceiving continuous artificial electrical stimulation.
  • By delivering 5-second electrical pulse bursts paired with 40-second recovery intervals, the team maintained a stable, unattenuated sensation of touch over 45 minutes across 60 trials.
  • Sources indicate that loss of tactile sensation in the hands, whether resulting from stroke, peripheral nerve injury, spinal trauma, or limb amputation, fundamentally impairs everyday activities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that biomedical engineers at Penn State have solved a major hurdle in neuroprosthetics and sensory rehabilitation: sensory habituation, where the brain gradually stops perceiving continuous artificial electrical stimulation. In a paper published in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, researchers led by Dr. Xiaogang Hu monitored cortical activity using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) during transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS).

By delivering 5-second electrical pulse bursts paired with 40-second recovery intervals, the team maintained a stable, unattenuated sensation of touch over 45 minutes across 60 trials. Neuroimaging revealed that while perception remained completely constant, the brain actively distributed tactile processing beyond the primary somatosensory cortex to wider neural networks.

Sources indicate that loss of tactile sensation in the hands, whether resulting from stroke, peripheral nerve injury, spinal trauma, or limb amputation, fundamentally impairs everyday activities. Basic tasks such as holding a fragile ceramic mug, grasping utensils, writing, or typing become daily battles when real-time sensory feedback is absent.

While bioengineers have developed transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS) and invasive neural implants capable of delivering artificial electrical pulses to mimic the sensation of touch, these technologies face a universal physiological barrier: sensory habituation.

Over extended periods, the central nervous system adapts to repetitive, artificial electrical stimulation. As neural circuits adjust to constant inputs, perceived intensity weakens and eventually fades away entirely. For an amputee using a motorized prosthetic hand, this decay is catastrophic: without steady tactile feedback, an individual cannot regulate grip force, leading them to either crush delicate objects or drop them unexpectedly.

It has been revealed that now, a team of researchers led by Dr. Xiaogang Hu, the Dorothy Foehr Huck and J. Lloyd Huck Chair in Neurorehabilitation and professor of mechanical engineering at Penn State, has uncovered both the neural dynamics of habituation and a stimulation protocol to bypass it.

Published in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, the study demonstrates that finely calibrated stimulation-and-rest intervals can preserve stable, long-term tactile sensations while triggering adaptive redistribution across the brain’s cerebral networks.

Industry observers note that “Repetitive stimulation — regardless of whether you engage stimulation through the nerves, skin or directly targeting a part of the brain — will be perceived as declining or weakening over time,” explained Dr. Hu, who holds joint appointments in Penn State’s Departments of Kinesiology and Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. “With this work, we are trying to avoid or minimize that habituation, enabling a more stable sense of touch over a longer timeframe.”.

To determine how electrical parameters influence neural adaptation, the researchers systematically tested varying electrical pulse durations and resting intervals across healthy volunteers.

In a recent development, electrodes were placed over peripheral nerves in the forearm to deliver mild electrical pulses designed to feel like a gentle tingling sensation. Using trial-by-trial psychophysical scoring, the team determined that a specific combination, 5 seconds of electrical stimulation followed by a 40-second recovery interval, prevented sensory decay.

When evaluated across an extended 45-minute continuous trial consisting of 60 consecutive stimulation cycles, participants reported zero habituation, retaining a crisp, consistent tactile sensation from the first pulse to the last.

“Picture someone is holding a cup of water with their prosthetic — the sensation of touch is critical for them to maintain an appropriate grip force,” Hu noted. “We don’t want them to crush the cup with too much force or for them to lose their sensation of touch over time and drop the cup; we need to ensure that the feeling is stable.”.

To explore how the brain maintains stable perception during prolonged stimulation, the investigators deployed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS).

Unlike functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which requires patients to lie immobilized inside a massive, noisy scanner bore, fNIRS employs a flexible cap equipped with lightweight optical optodes. These emitters project harmless beams of near-infrared light through the scalp and skull into the superficial cerebral cortex. By measuring how light reflects back to paired photodetectors, the system quantifies local shifts in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin, serving as a high-fidelity proxy for localized neuronal metabolism and synaptic activity.

Targeting the primary somatosensory cortex (the cerebral hub responsible for mapping bodily touch), fNIRS captured real-time cortical dynamics while participants sat upright and received TNS.

The optical scans uncovered an unexpected neurofunctional divergence: while participants reported that the physical sensation felt identical across all 45 minutes, their underlying brain activation patterns were constantly shifting.

Recent findings suggest that “Participants report that the sensation feels the same, but the active regions in their brain actually change over time, with changing intensity of activation and spatial distribution,” said first author Dr. Susan Coltman, assistant professor at the University of Guelph, who conducted the study as a postdoctoral researcher in Hu’s lab. “The signals start out in the somatosensory cortex, but over time, they move out beyond that origin area to different regions of the brain, reflecting progressive recruitment of distributed brain regions to process information during prolonged sensory stimulation.”.

Rather than a static, local response, sensory preservation appears to depend on the brain dynamically recruiting distributed associative and secondary sensory networks to sustain conscious perception.

Recent findings suggest that these findings carry major implications for clinical neurorehabilitation. Individuals recovering from hemispheric stroke or living with upper-limb amputations already experience extensive cortical reorganization. Understanding how the healthy brain balances stimulation timing and network recruitment provides a quantitative template for programming next-generation bionic prostheses and wearable rehabilitation sleeves.

The research team intends to extend these optimized stimulation paradigms into patient populations with focal stroke lesions and limb loss, aiming to calibrate personalized electrical intervals that accommodate damaged, rewired neural pathways.

By striking the biological balance between stimulation and recovery, engineers are moving closer to artificial limbs that don’t just move naturally, but feel permanently real.

What is sensory habituation in nerve stimulation?

Sensory habituation occurs when the nervous system becomes accustomed to continuous, repetitive artificial electrical stimulation, causing the perceived sensation of touch to gradually weaken and fade away over time.

How did the Penn State team prevent habituation during nerve stimulation?

The researchers identified an optimized timing ratio: applying 5 seconds of mild electrical stimulation followed by a 40-second rest period. This cycle allowed peripheral nerves and central circuits to recover, sustaining a completely stable sense of touch over 45 minutes and 60 cycles.

How did brain activity change during the experiment?

Although participants felt the exact same level of sensation throughout the 45-minute window, fNIRS imaging showed that active brain regions shifted over time. Brain activity originated in the primary somatosensory cortex and then progressively migrated outward, recruiting wider distributed brain networks to sustain sensory processing.

Funding & Support: Supported by the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research (NIDILRR) and the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Division of Information and Intelligent Systems (grants IIS-2330862 and IIS-2319139).

fNIRS Characterization of Temporal Potentiation During Optimized Nerve Stimulation.

Restoring stable somatosensory feedback through transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS) represents a significant challenge in neural engineering; however, the cortical dynamics underlying sustained stimulation are not yet well characterized.

This study utilizes a multi-method functional near-infrared spectroscopy framework to quantify the temporal evolution of cortical engagement during temporally structured TNS. It was hypothesized that stimulation parameters fundamentally constrain the spatiotemporal profile of the hemodynamic response function.

Recent findings suggest that A General Linear Model with temporal and dispersion derivatives was used to analyze hemodynamic responses in 10 participants across three phases: validation, duration optimization (2, 5, or 10 seconds), and sustained engagement (45 minutes). During the optimization phase, 5-second stimulation produced the highest canonical amplitude with optimal dispersion characteristics, while 10-second trains resulted in significant temporal delays.

According to recent reports, during the sustained phase, parametric modeling indicated no linear decay in cortical response. Instead, the cortex demonstrated temporal potentiation, characterized by a transition from sparse early-phase activation to widespread late-phase recruitment across the sensorimotor network. The left posterior parietal cortex (BA5) served as a continuous integration hub, whereas primary somatosensory regions exhibited dynamic late-onset engagement.

Industry observers note that these findings characterize a nonlinear temporal potentiation pattern, demonstrating that the selected stimulation/rest timing regime can sustain cortical engagement and facilitate delayed network expansion. The observed intersubject heterogeneity highlights the necessity for adaptive, closed-loop TNS controllers guided by real-time hemodynamic biomarkers.

We’ve all been there. January 1st hits, and you decide this is the year you’re going to change your life and become the best version of yourself with some Newly introduced Year’s resolutions. You might optimistically think, “You know what? I’m going to be healthier this year! I’m only going to drink on the weekends.”.

Then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine. You’re instantly filled with regret for breaking your resolution and vow to never do them again because they don’t work and are clearly designed to make you feel disappointed.

So let’s ditch our list of impossible goals and jump into 60 resolutions that could help you thrive in 2027.

At the end of the year, many of us step back and realize that we feel really disconnected from a lot of the people in our life. We get busy and stuck in our own little world. It’s too easy for connections with our family, friends, partners, or coworkers to dwindle from time to time.

Industry observers note that when someone’s talking to you, focus fully on what they’re saying instead of thinking about your reply or what you’re going to eat for your next meal (we’ve all been there). Active listening highlights respect to your loved one and can help deepen your bond. If you want to get better at active listening, here are eight techniques to help.

Too often, we take those around us for granted, so let the people in your life know you appreciate them. Saying something as easy as, “thank you” or writing a cute little note can let your loved one know how much they mean to you and make them feel good. Who doesn’t want to make their loved one feel good?

If you love them, say it. Life’s too short! Telling someone you love them is powerful and can help you grow a stronger bond. If you have people in your life like a macho uncle or disengaged cousin who have a hard time saying I love you, be the first to jump in and show them that it’s okay to express your affection for one another.

Recent findings suggest that if you notice someone struggling in your life, step in and help. It doesn't need to be revolutionary. It could be helping with laundry or simply being there to listen. Just letting them know that you see their efforts and want to help can make a huge difference.

According to recent reports, relationships are work. And in order for them to work, you need to put time into them. So set a reminder to check in with your loved ones, especially the ones you don’t see often. A quick text or call can do the trick and help you stay connected with your favorite people. And if you have folks in your life who are struggling, or who experience loneliness, make an extra effort to reach out and show you care.

It has been revealed that don’t let misunderstandings grow. When you’re upset with someone, bring it up to them calmly and kindly, and with the goal of finding a solution. It can help to lead with “I feel” statements. And if your feelings are hurt over an innocent misunderstanding, start with, “I know you didn’t mean to hurt my feelings but,” so the other person knows they’re not in trouble and you want to come to a place of understanding.

Recent findings suggest that this might sound obvious, but if your loved one has good news, show genuine excitement for the good things that are happening for them. We all feel good when others celebrate with us. So send those flowers — almost no one’s going to get mad at you for sending flowers. Sometimes celebrating success for others feels hard if you feel stuck in your life, but by genuinely finding happiness for others, you may feel the glow of that happiness yourself.

Sources indicate that use conversions with others as a time to genuinely disconnect from technology and focus on being together. When you’re spending time with someone, keep your phone in your pocket, in your purse, or somewhere that’s not in your hand. Give your loved one your full attention. This will make them feel seen and it helps you to stay more in the moment and form deeper connections.

Everyone loves to feel seen and valued. Sometimes just surprising someone you love with a small gesture can make their day. It doesn’t have to be big, it could just be showing up to a hang with your loved one’s favorite snack, their preferred coffee drink, or even a small bouquet of flowers. Trying to be better about budgeting? Handwritten cards, or homemade crafts also make lovely surprises.

According to recent reports, when someone you care about is struggling, before reacting, take a moment to put yourself in their shoes and understand what they might be going through. This can be a lot easier said than done, but try to treat them the way you would want to be treated —  with kindness instead of judgment.

We all have preferences for how we like to give and receive love and it’s so special when the people in our lives make an effort to communicate affection in the ways we most appreciate. (And probably earn you brownie points!).

According to recent reports, say yes to an invite or an activity you wouldn’t normally do. Stepping out of your comfort zone can help you feel energized and open you up to upcoming experiences and learnings about yourself. The one time when it’s okay not to say yes is if you’re establishing boundaries with your emotional energy or time. It’s all about balance!

Industry observers note that while saying yes is great (see above), saying no is also important. Make an effort to have healthy relationships with solid boundaries. Tell people what you need, like alone time or limits on work talk. And respect their boundaries too. If all of that sounds tough, check out these six tips to setting healthy boundaries in your relationships.

Sources indicate that humans make mistakes and the best thing you can do is to acknowledge them, learn and grow. So try to take responsibility if you make a mistake. You’ll feel free of guilt and you won’t have to double down on something you probably didn’t mean to do in the first place (like a bad joke that hurt someone’s feelings, or a meeting you were super late for.) A heartfelt apology can mend any damage and show your maturity (these seven tips will help you do it).

Doesn’t it feel like we’re always trying to find a better work-life balance, get promoted, improve our work ethic, and feel more fulfilled with the work we’re doing? That constant desire for some sort of growth or change can be overwhelming and leave you not knowing where to start.

So we’ve put together 15 work resolutions that might be more sustainable and rewarding for you — and will hopefully make the whole process feel less overwhelming.

According to recent reports, protecting your personal time is so key for avoiding burnout, so decide on clear work hours and stick to them. Try setting a goal for logging off by 6pm or not looking at emails in your off time. If your job doesn’t at the moment give you the freedom to set these boundaries, chat with your superiors and express your goals where work-life balance is concerned.

Organize your workspace to reduce clutter. A working area that you like (or at least doesn’t cause more stress) can really improve your mood and your focus. Once you reduce the clutter and get rid of any items that aren’t sparking joy, you could mindfully add things that feel good like a plant, photo, or a comfy chair.

Recent findings suggest that large projects can be overwhelming. Try breaking them down into smaller, more manageable steps to make them less daunting and help you stay on track. You can also practice time-boxing to keep your focus — here’s how to do it .

In a recent development, go for a five-minute walk, enjoy a cup or tea, or do a quick stretch. Just like you want to celebrate the achievements of the people in your life, it’s equally notable to celebrate yourself! Take note of all of your accomplishments. This can help boost your confidence, help you stay motivated, and even make you smile.

Making fresh friends isn’t just for your school years. Make an effort to connect with coworkers or other people in your field. Getting coffee with colleagues can help you build relationships and even help with career growth. You might find that your career is more fulfilling when you have solid relationships with colleagues and coworkers.

Work on being clear and concise in emails, meetings, and in conversations. Practicing good communication not only improves your productivity but also helps avoid misunderstandings (these 13 tips can help).

If you’re overwhelmed and juggling too much, look for tasks that can be given to others to make your life easier. This doesn’t mean you’re not good at your job. It just means you're making sure your energy is spent where it’s needed most.

Recent findings suggest that struggling to focus? Single-tasting is where it’s at. Take on one task at a time and not five at once. This will improve the quality of your work and help you feel less like you want to scream.

Even if it’s scary, seek out feedback from your boss, coworkers, or clients. Constructive input can help you get better and show that you want to improve. Just make sure you’re also receiving feedback for things you’re doing well, not just areas where you could do better.

It has been revealed that find a method that helps you stay on top of deadlines. A to-do list app, a daily planner, or a bullet journal could help keep track of all your tasks. Explore some different ideas to find what works best for you.

Don’t hesitate to ask for what you need. If anything, this can help you get taken more seriously and help with career growth. Ask for that raise, request that more flexible schedule, tell your boss you need additional resources to complete that project.

Recent findings suggest that set goals that align with your long-term dreams and values, not just what you hope to achieve. These could be around building confidence, becoming a more mindful leader, or exploring a new field you’ve always been interested in.

Industry observers note that when you don’t feel mentally like you’re firing on all cylinders, it can be tough to even think of what to focus on to help your mental health. Recent findings suggest that (Psst: You don’t have to do all of them. Start with one or two that’ll help you feel more balanced, calm, and connected, and then go from there.).

According to recent reports, write down and reflect on your thoughts, feelings, and experiences each day. This can help you process your emotions and recognize some patterns you have. Journaling is also a great way to practice gratitude.

According to recent reports, each day, take a moment to think of three things you’re grateful for. This can rewire your brain to look for the positives in your life. It doesn’t have to be getting a promotion or finding your perfect partner, it can be as small as not burning your bagel today. If you want to find more ways to incorporate gratitude into your days, here are eight ideas to get you started.

Sources indicate that spend a few minutes a day practicing mindfulness. And while this could be a five minute meditation, it could also be a bit of deep breathing on a work break, or just noticing the sights and sounds on your morning walk. Any moment where you become fully present counts!

Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help you get better quality sleep (here are six more tips to help you get those Zzzzs). The more rested you are, the more you’ll be able to handle the stress that comes up throughout the day.

Sources indicate that nature has a way of calming us down and recharging us, so if it’s possible, try to get outside everyday. It doesn't have to be a big hike, it can be as simple as walking around your block or even just going into your yard.

Industry observers note that this is a big one! Try to gradually reduce the time you spend on your phone, computer, or watching TV, especially before bed. You could read that novel that’s been on your bedside table for ever or catch up with a loved one instead. But take it slow, we know it’s not easy.

Give yourself permission to say no to things that overwhelm or overcommit you. It’s more crucial to protect your energy than to burn yourself out trying to please other people. If saying no is hard for you, here’s 30 ways to do it nicely.

Get in the habit of reaching out to a loved one or a therapist when you’re feeling stressed or overwhelmed. Talking about our feelings can help us feel lighter and even give us a newly introduced perspective.

Industry observers note that A clean environment isn’t just for your desk. Having a clean home can calm you too. So take some small steps to organize your home. You might try doing just one room at a time, it doesn’t need to be all at once.

Schedule regular breaks so you don’t have a meltdown. These pauses can really help you reduce your stress and keep you focused. Grabbing a glass of water, breathing deeply, or gently stretching can all help reset you and give your mind a moment to rest.

Recent findings suggest that treat yourself the way you would your closest friend. Avoid going in on yourself with harsh, critical thoughts and instead say some sweet nothings to yourself. We know this isn’t always easy, so here are eight tips to help you quiet that inner critic.

Start a hobby that lets you express yourself. This can be therapeutic and put you in a better mood. Ever been curious about painting or playing music? Maybe now’s your chance to explore that curiosity.

Exercising relieves a lot of stress. But you don’t need to spend hours at the gym or set some substantial weight loss goal. Instead, try out a new yoga class, have a dance party in your living room, or find other ways to move your body that feel nourishing to you.

According to recent reports, go easy on yourself, you don’t need to be perfect (newsflash: there’s no such thing). It can help to focus on all the small ways you're growing each day, not on the destination. Sometimes it’s better to think about growth-setting instead of goal setting.

Don’t regularly spend your time on something that drains your energy. Seek out places that bring you positivity instead. If certain people you hang around with make you feel bad, limit your exposure to them. This might look like setting boundaries with family about how many events you attend each year, or with friends by limiting how much you talk or get together.

It has been revealed that okay, let’s face it. Most of us want to look and feel our best — and there’s nothing wrong with that. But better physical health is also about feeling energized, staying strong, and giving our body the help it needs to thrive.

It has been revealed that we don’t need to tell you that working out consistently is a lot easier said than done. Sure, in a perfect world, we always have the time and energy to get to the gym. But we don’t live in that world. We have endless responsibilities and working out might be the first thing to go when we’re busy.

So explore these 15 manageable resolutions that can help you feel strong and energized going into 2027. And remember, you don’t need to force yourself to go all-in on physical wellness to feel better. Just start with one or two that feel like they’d be easier to make a consistent habit and go from there.

Aim for some form of movement every day –– it doesn’t have to be intense. Try a 10–minute stretch or a brisk walk through your favorite part of your neighborhood. Focus on what makes you feel good in your body, which may change day to day.

Hydration makes you feel good and stay alert, so try to aim for 8–10 glasses of water a day. Carry a reusable water bottle with you to make it easier to hit your goal and remind you to drink. If regular water feels boring try adding slices of your favorite citrus or fresh mint to your water.

In a recent development, add a rainbow of foods to your plate! Focus on eating a mix of fruits, veggies, lean proteins, and whole grains. Recent findings suggest that working out can really feel like work a lot of the time. So shake up your routine to help keep you excited to exercise. Ever tried kickboxing or swimming? Maybe 2027 is the year you hop in the boxing ring or jump in the pool.

Recent findings suggest that if you have a desk job, try to stand up and move every hour. Consider switching to a standing desk if that’s an option. If you work from home and have space for a walking pad in front of a standing desk you can also get your steps in while you work.

In a recent development, good posture helps prevent back and neck pain so pay attention to how you sit and stand. And add exercises that focus on strengthening your core into your workout. This will help support better alignment. Sitting at a desk for work? Set alarms every so often to remind you to stand up and stretch.

Industry observers note that celebrating your progress helps you to keep going — we all need a good pat on the back. If you drink an extra glass of water or walk an extra mile, take note of it. Maybe even do a little happy dance. If you go for a walk four days in a row, make a note in your journal or notebook. The more you celebrate your progress the prouder of yourself you’ll be (and the easier it is to keep it up).

💙 Learn how to celebrate the Small Wins on the path to achieving your larger goals with help from Jay Shetty.

Fresh Year’s resolutions are personal goals or promises you make to yourself at the start of a new year. They can be about anything and it’s entirely up to you. They can be big like training for a marathon or small like drinking more water.

Usually people use it as a chance to reflect, change up some patterns in their life, and start fresh. If you’re looking to set a resolution but don’t know where to start, here are five areas people tend to focus on:.

In a recent development, you don’t have to make resolutions to have a wonderful new year. But if you want to try, keep in mind that resolutions work best when you make them work for you. So yes — resolutions matter if you use them as a tool to help you live with more purpose and joy, then you’ll set yourself up for more success.

It has been revealed that when you’re setting your resolutions, focus on what would make you feel happier, healthier and more fulfilled and go from there. And approach resolutions with kindness and flexibility, especially if you don’t end up following through on one.

According to recent reports, if the idea of resolutions feels overwhelming — we get it. Here’s three ways that could make it easier for you:.

Focus on one word or theme for the year that feels right to you, like “balance” or “growth.”.

Set a small monthly intention instead of a year-long commitment.

Celebrate progress instead of perfection by noticing little wins along the way.

According to recent reports, we wish there were five magical resolutions that could solve all of our problems at once. But unfortunately there’s no such thing. What we can tell you is the most successful resolutions tend to be the ones that feel right to you.

It’s vital to focus on the right area when setting your resolution, so you’ll be more likely to stick with them. Here are five areas to focus on when setting your resolution:.

Resolutions that focus on building stronger relationships — Pick ones that’ll fill you up and add more joy to your life.

Resolutions that focus on taking care of your physical health — Pick ones that focus on regular exercise, better nutrition, or improved sleep.

Resolutions that focus on your mental health — Pick ones that practice gratitude or mindfulness, so that they can help you feel calmer and more balanced.

Resolutions that focus on your career –– Pick ones that focus on learning a upcoming skill or creating a better work-life balance so that your professional life can become more rewarding.

Resolutions that focus on personal growth –– Pick ones that focus on starting upcoming hobbies or giving back to your community.

It has been revealed that all of us at one point or another have probably failed at a resolution we’ve set for ourselves. And when that happens, it can feel pretty disappointing. But resolutions can work — if you set them in the right way.

Resolutions that are vague or overly ambitious tend to be a recipe for failure. But if you set ones that are realistic and meaningful to you, it’ll be a lot easier to keep your resolution and see the change you want. But remember to be flexible and kind to yourself. We’re all not perfect and mistakes happen. So try not to beat yourself up if you don’t stick to your goals perfectly. Focus on progress, not perfection.

If you find it easier to set monthly intentions as opposed to setting one year-long resolution, go for that. Tailor the resolutions so they work best for you.

Sometimes the minute we think of resolutions, we can get sad or overwhelmed at the baggage of our past failed resolutions. If this is you — we understand. Resolutions aren’t for everyone. But if you’re interested, there are other ways you can focus on self-improvement and growth.

If a long list of goals is too daunting for you, try picking a single word to guide your year. You could use words like “balance,” or “connection,” to remind yourself to make choices that match with your values.

If setting smaller, short-term goals might help you to stay motivated, you could try focusing on building better sleep habits in January, and then shifting to something like improving your diet in February.

According to recent reports, if tracking your progress will make it more fun for you and help you to invest more, try using a habit tracker app, or even just a calendar. This way it’ll be easier to celebrate your little wins along the way.

Resolutions that focus on relationships can bring more connection, understanding, and happiness into your life. And a good way to show the people you love the most how much they mean to you is to set a resolution to spend more quality time with them.

Recent findings suggest that acts of kindness also go a long way to strengthen your relationships. So if this is crucial to you, try setting an intention to express gratitude more often, like thanking your partner for their support.

It has been revealed that you could also set a resolution to unplug more often. This can help free up your time and create more meaningful, distraction-free moments with the people you care about the most.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care. Instead, the doctor provides care when close friends need help or when an emergency occurs in their presence. While these acts are good in and of themselves, one could not help but wonder whether the doctor’s approach maximizes their potential positive impact.

In a recent development, positive psychologists often act like that. Like the doctor, we have specialized knowledge. We run studies and test theories. We accomplish things in our smaller circles. But without diminishing the value of these acts, one cannot help—as with our imaginary doctor—but wonder whether we could sometimes do more.

While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue. Public policymakers are, to some degree, in need of the very thing we can (but often do not) provide.

In a recent development, consider that public policy creators confront conflicting requests. Some voices ask for dismantling of camps for the unhoused, while others favor leniency. Some want programming to address the mental health of all schoolkids, while others worry these programs distract from education or may even be harmful. Others want more dollars for police enforcement while still others want less. Policy creators thus often want guidance. Absent guidance, they might follow their intuition or the most confident-sounding “researcher.” Psychologists can help.

Sources indicate that how best to help? In this piece, we briefly explore three ways that positive psychology can impact public policy.

Public officials often focus on brass-tacks complications such as better housing, education, transit, recreation opportunities, or public safety.

However, their impact on well-being is an implicit goal in almost all of those. People want better housing and transit so they can live happier lives. They want to be safe so that the subjective quality of their lives improves. Curiously, however, well-being is often omitted from formal discussion in policy procedures. It is everywhere and nowhere at the same time: It forms the backbone of almost every policy aim and yet is less often pursued in its own right.

It has been revealed that why is that? We suspect it is because the brass-tacks problems have measurable outcomes—and policymakers perceive that “well-being” is too ephemeral to be measured.

Sources indicate that that’s where psychologists, and perhaps especially positive psychologists, can help. Well-being no longer represents an unmeasurable ephemeral concept. The field has produced and refined legitimate scientific tools. Indeed, when we started in psychology, measures of personality and many other variables were well-established, but measures of well-being were treated with some suspicion. Since then, many studies have supported the value of well-being measures.

As a result, one way we as psychologists can improve public policy is to consistently remind policymakers that well-being can be measured just like housing costs or educational tests scores. Well-being measurement is not some elusive Platonic ideal—we can find well-validated tools that assess which factors facilitate flourishing along many dimensions, including hedonic, eudaimonic, physical health, and generic happiness (for a review of some, see our 2016 overview).

Thus, when policymakers turn to the academy for recommendations, we can put front and center our history of measurement of well-being. When studying the impact of a training program in a shelter for people who lack housing, psychological well-being of those receiving the treatment can be measured rather than measuring only items designed to facilitate well-being. Current public policy challenges are often framed in well-being terms—and we have tools needed to provide policy recommendations. From the effects of artificial intelligence to social media usage, an array of studies exist showing the validity of our well-being tools in aiding policymakers.

One of us has often asked students to guess which psychological variables are most strongly associated with psychological well-being. None of the students have ever guessed “generalized trust,” even though trust consistently predicts well-being, with effects as large as many more widely known measures.

Indeed, generalized trust receives limited attention among academics (for exceptions, see some of the World Happiness Reports). Policymakers, too, often underestimate the importance of trust, so one way to influence policy is to remind policymakers of the importance of building trust in order to enable flourishing. Both general trust (e.g., “Do you think most people would return money to the owner if they found a wallet containing $200?”) and institutional trust (e.g., “Do you think the government can be trusted?” “Do you think corporations are corrupt?”) have surprisingly strong relations with well-being. Trust facilitates community, relations with neighbors, and conversations with strangers.

It has been revealed that misperceptions often create mistrust. For example, most people underestimate the proportion of others who act in trustworthy ways, as when most people underestimate how many individuals will return money found in lost wallets. Policymakers would be well-served to understand the difference between mistrust based on false perceptions and that which is at least partly justified, and psychologists are well-placed to help with that. Highlighting the trust findings can help policymakers focus on policies most likely to matter.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes those policies can focus on correcting misperceptions. Consider, though, what hurts trust among people. Mistrust can emerge when publicized incidents provoke fear; for example, if public spaces become truly more dangerous, then trust will decline.

According to recent reports, positive psychologists study three main topics: positive emotional states (i.e., well-being), positive traits (i.e., virtue and character), and positive institutions. Remember the third. Work with institutions. They help define your society.

Recent findings suggest that in our graduate studies, we received no training on collaborating with public institutions. A few strategies have helped us greatly:.

Their guide suggests, for example, that elected leaders and government administrators often won’t read even short written summaries of policy-relevant research that academics provide. However, those same leaders might:.

Initially, that sounded nonsensical to us, and disappointing after our many hours writing brief engaging summaries of research! Now, these recommendations are in accord with our observations. These interactions matter.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve also learned that government-funded institutions often have limited education budgets for their staff but want to do training. If you gain respect, they may be open to you providing training to their leaders. If you don’t present your conclusions, others, who might lack a scientific foundation, will present theirs.

Industry observers note that you can proceed with the confidence earned by well-validated science, but also mention qualifications or uncertainty. Policymakers often prefer simple answers, so social pressure discourages intellectual humility. Don’t let that preference for simplicity capture your thinking. We may be trusted more in the long run by presenting our data while admitting uncertainties or exceptions.

Let’s return to a medical metaphor. In medicine, if a prostate cancer test correctly identified 90% of men who have prostate cancer, but only 2% of men had prostate cancer, then the odds are that many positives would be false positives; in fact, most positives would probably be false positives.

In a recent development, that potential error does not disqualify the test—but ignoring the error would have bad consequences for everyone. Likewise, if our measures of well-being or measures of ill-being become widely used to screen students for further attention, we could recommend a test confidently and yet also need to continually remind users of the frequency of errors. Overdiagnosis could change student perceptions in unhealthy ways. Neglecting to emphasize the errors could harm people and undermine our credibility.

Adopt a strategy of confidence in the science while providing frequent reminders of necessary qualifications.

#51. Pablo Neruda on How to Hold Time

Pablo Neruda on How to Hold Time

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “Time is a river that sweeps me along, but I am a river,” Borges wrote.
  • Sources indicate that most of us are not Borges.
  • And all the while, our time is nested within our times — the epoch we are living through together, born into it with no more choice in the matter than the body and brain and family we have been born into.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “Time is a river that sweeps me along, but I am a river,” Borges wrote. “Time is a fire that consumes me, but I am the fire.”.

Sources indicate that most of us are not Borges. Most of us are drowning in bewilderment at where the time goes, burning with the urgency of being alive while waiting to start living, wandering the labyrinth of life with wayward presence, wishing that time ran differently as the cult of productivity turns each minute into a blade pressed against the vein of our transience.

And all the while, our time is nested within our times — the epoch we are living through together, born into it with no more choice in the matter than the body and brain and family we have been born into. In his magnificent essay on Shakespeare, James Baldwin countered the commonplace lament of every epoch: “It is noted that his time was easier than ours, but I doubt it — no time can be easy if one is living through it.” A century before him — a century of unrest and transformation — Emerson issued the ultimate antilamentation: “This time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but know what to do with it.”.

Recent findings suggest that not knowing what to do with the time we have been given, not knowing how to hold time in our personal and political lives, is at bottom an act of forgetting how time hold us. Pablo Neruda (July 12, 1904–September 23, 1973) casts a spell against forgetting in the fourth canto of his long poem “Morning,”:.

You will remember that whimsical ravine where the vibrant aromas rose, and from time to time a bird dressed in water and languor: winter’s garment.

You will remember those gifts from the earth: piquing fragrance, gold clay, thickets of herbs, wild roots, bewitching thorns like swords.

You will remember the bouquet you brought, a bouquet of shadow and silent water, a bouquet like foam-covered stone.

And that time was like never and always: We go where nothing is expected and find everything waiting there.

In a recent development, if time is the fundamental problem of human life and poetry is our most precise technology for parsing the aching astonishment of being alive, then time is the prime subject of poetry. Neruda knew this — time is the subterranean current coursing beneath his vast and varied body of work, the substrate upon which all of his stunning love poems and his meditations on the inner life grow. He reverenced the stones for how they have “touched time,” reverenced the minute for how it is “bound to join the river of time that bears us,” reverenced “the inexhaustible springs of time,” longed for “a time complete as an ocean,” then made that ocean with his poetry.

In his poem “The Enigmas,” composed during WWII, he writes:.

You’ve asked me what the crustacean spins between its gold claws and I reply: the sea knows.

You wonder what the sea squirt waits for in its transparent bell? What does it wait for?

I’ll tell you: it’s waiting for time like you.

A decade later, in one of his “Elemental Odes,” Neruda laid out his most explicit instruction for how to hold time:.

Sources indicate that listen and learn. Time is divided into two rivers: one flows backward, devouring life already lived; the other moves forward with you exposing your life. For a single second they may be joined. Now. This is that moment, the drop of an instant that washes away the past. It is the present. It is in your hands. Racing, slipping, tumbling like a waterfall. But it is yours. Help it grow with love, with firmness, with stone and flight, with resounding rectitude, with purest grains, the most brilliant metal from your heart, walking in the full light of day without fear of truth, goodness, justice, companions of song, time that flows will have the shape and sound of a guitar, and when you want to bow to the past, the singing spring of transparent time will reveal your wholeness. Time is joy.

Couple with three poems for trusting time, then revisit Kahlil Gibran on how to befriend time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two newly introduced studies suggest autism and ADHD are becoming better recognized, not actually more prevalent, and that executive function and social challenges seen in both conditions actually stem from different underlying brain mechanisms.

ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) share overlapping symptoms, and prior studies suggest that nearly half of autistic children also have ADHD.1 Now, two new studies on ADHD and ASD profiles suggest that rising diagnosis rates are a product of improved symptom recognition and diagnostic practices, and that executive function and social impairments seen in both ADHD and ASD may be traced to different cognitive pathways.

In a recent development, the first study, published in JAMA Psychiatry,2 evaluated the health records of 71,000 children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and 713,000 controls; it found that the annual number of individuals in the nationwide Danish health registry with newly diagnosed ADHD and/or ASD increased from 4,944 in 2012 to 9,179 in 2022. The proportion of girls diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and the median age at diagnosis also grew during the 10-year study period from 2012 to 2022.

However, traditional risk factors strongly linked to an ADHD or ASD diagnosis in 2012, such as low birth weight or lower household income, have become progressively less predictive with time. For example, children born with a low birth weight were 54% more likely to receive a subsequent diagnosis of ADHD or ASD in 2012; by 2022, that percentage dropped to 17%. Overall, the study found that children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD today more closely resemble their neurotypical peers compared to those diagnosed 10 years ago.

In a recent development, these findings do not mean that ADHD or ASD has become less impairing; the spectrum of cases has shifted as clinicians get better at identifying less obvious cases. Greater awareness of ADHD and ASD, and broader access to diagnostic assessment tools, are also factors contributing to growing diagnoses among children.

“The study results do not show that these conditions are being overdiagnosed, or that they have become less severe,” indicates Oleguer Plana-Ripoll, Ph.D., a senior author of the study. “Rather, they indicate that the population receiving these diagnoses has changed over time, and this needs to be taken into account when interpreting current trends.”.

The second, smaller study, published in Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry,3 found that executive functioning (EF) and social cognition (SC) impairments in children diagnosed with ADHD or ASD may look similar, but the impairments stem from different underlying mechanisms.

The cross-sectional, four-year study analyzed performance-based measures of 123 children, aged 6 to 11 years, across three matched groups: mild ASD, combined-type ADHD, and neurotypical peers.

Findings indicated that both ADHD and ASD groups performed worse than their neurotypical peers on measures of EF and SC. However, children with ADHD demonstrated weak social cognition due to difficulties with response inhibition and attention. Social cognition weaknesses in children with ASD, on the other hand, appeared to result from difficulties in understanding and interpreting social information.

More specifically, children in the ASD group performed significantly worse than children with ADHD on measures of:.

Children with ASD also displayed more difficulties than did children with ADHD on executive function tasks that measured the ability to shift between rules and adapt strategies.

Children in the ADHD group performed significantly worse than those in the ASD group on measures of:.

According to recent reports, how executive functions related to social cognition across disorders was the strongest indication of different cognitive processes between the two clinical groups. In the ADHD group, the theory-of-mind model explained 72% of the variance, compared to just 55% in the ASD group.

According to recent reports, the researchers surmise that a person with ADHD relies heavily on executive functions, such as inhibition, auditory attention, and design fluency, for social cognition. In essence, their difficulties in social situations are not because they don’t understand social concepts but because distractions and impulsivity interfere.

In the ASD group, social difficulties were more likely to stem from affect recognition (understanding facial cues) and response set (cognitive flexibility, shifting perspectives), rather than from attention deficit or impulse control.

In a recent development, “ADHD and autism are two separate and distinct conditions that happen to be found together much more frequently than would be expected by chance alone,” says ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. “For people with co-existing ADHD and ASD, treating the ADHD is a means to an end. The world is a classroom for people with ASD, and they have to be ready to observe and practice what they’ve learned.”.

Results from the study suggest individuals would benefit more from targeted ADHD and ASD interventions matched to each disorder-specific profile rather than a single shared approach.

Blood-Brain Barrier Protein Atlas Unlocks Alzheimer’s

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a study published in Cell, researchers at Gladstone Institutes have created the first comprehensive atlas of circulating blood proteins that cross the blood-brain barrier into the brain. Led by Dr. Andrew Yang, the team deployed Nobel Prize-winning protein-labeling chemistry to track 861 plasma proteins in mice, finding that the blood-brain barrier selectively imports just 92, most originating in distant organs like the liver.

In preclinical models of Alzheimer’s disease, researchers discovered that before the barrier physically degrades and leaks toxins, it first shuts down the import of critical protective proteins, such as liver-derived apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1). Boosting systemic APOA1 restored neuronal connectivity and halted disease progression, demonstrating that neurodegeneration may begin when the brain’s peripheral molecular supply line is severed.

Source: Gladstone Institutes / Cell.

For more than a century, neuroscientists have viewed the blood-brain barrier (BBB) primarily as a physiological fortress: a tight seal of endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytic end-feet designed to keep pathogens, peripheral immune cells, and toxic macromolecules out of delicate cerebral tissue.

However, this fortress model fails to explain how the brain monitors systemic physiology or obtains essential large-molecule signals generated by peripheral organs like the liver and kidneys.

Sources indicate that in a landmark study published in the journal Cell, researchers at Gladstone Institutes overturn this one-way defensive paradigm. Led by Gladstone Investigator Dr. Andrew Yang, the team mapped the first comprehensive atlas of blood-borne proteins transported across the blood-brain barrier into the mammalian brain.

Their findings reveal that the BBB functions as a selective molecular transfer hub, using specialized receptors to sample plasma proteins from distant bodily organs and direct them to specific brain cells using an intrinsic molecular “ZIP code” system.

Critically, the research demonstrates that in Alzheimer’s disease, this supply line breaks down long before the barrier becomes physically porous, opening therapeutic strategies aimed at treating neurodegeneration from the outside in.

Industry observers note that different visceral organs continuously secrete cocktails of signaling proteins into blood plasma to reflect systemic metabolic states. Yet, identifying which of these proteins cross intact cerebral vessels without disrupting normal vascular physiology has historically proven technically impossible.

To solve this, Yang’s team utilized bioorthogonal, click-chemistry protein-labeling strategies to tag the entire mouse plasma proteome without altering biological binding properties.

After infusing labeled plasma proteins back into the circulation of mice, the researchers analyzed cerebral tissue to map which molecules successfully traversed the barrier:.

It has been revealed that “We think of blood proteins as messengers carrying signals from distant body parts, and the cells of the blood-brain barrier import only the ones the brain really needs,” explained first author Dr. Haoyue Zhou, a postdoctoral fellow in Yang’s laboratory. “It’s like a molecular ZIP code system that helps each protein reach its intended destination.”.

A prime example identified in the atlas is apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1). Synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes in the liver, APOA1 travels through the circulation, crosses the BBB, and targets astrocytes. Once bound, it activates signaling cascades required to maintain synaptic density and stabilize neuronal connectivity.

Sources indicate that “For a century, we’ve treated the blood-brain barrier as a simple physical boundary protecting the brain from toxins,” said Dr. Yang, assistant professor of neurology at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) and investigator at Gladstone. “We’re finding that it’s an intelligent interface that plucks the right proteins in the blood, often from distant parts of the body, and delivers them to the right cell types in the brain. Brain health depends on this sophisticated molecular supply line from the body.”.

The team next tracked this transport machinery across the lifespan in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease.

The prevailing view in neurovascular research holds that Alzheimer’s progression causes the blood-brain barrier to physically disintegrate, opening tight junctions and allowing toxic albumin and fibrinogen to flood the parenchyma, sparking neuroinflammation.

However, Yang and Zhou discovered that an opposing failure occurs first:.

Sources indicate that “Before the barrier starts leaking harmful proteins into the brain, it stops letting the beneficial ones through,” Zhou noted. “The brain’s supply line from the body starts to fail.”.

To test whether replenishing these lost peripheral signals could counteract neurodegeneration, the researchers engineered Alzheimer’s mouse models to overexpress human APOA1 specifically in their liver tissue.

As circulating levels increased, more APOA1 crossed the blood-brain barrier into the central nervous system. The influx of liver-derived APOA1 restored astrocytic support, preserved synaptic connectivity, and reduced cognitive and behavioral signs of Alzheimer’s disease.

Industry observers note that “Alzheimer’s disease may not start entirely inside the brain; it may start when the brain’s supply line from the body is severed,” Yang concluded. “If that’s right, we may be able to fight this disease from outside the brain, by restoring what the brain has lost.”.

According to recent reports, the identification of this 92-protein atlas provides dual translational opportunities. First, clinicians could potentially treat cognitive decline by pharmacologically boosting protective protein production in peripheral organs like the liver. Second, by mapping the precise endogenous receptors used by these 92 proteins, bioengineers can design targeted “molecular shuttles” that piggyback life-saving therapeutics across the blood-brain barrier directly to diseased brain cells.

What is the fresh blood-brain barrier protein atlas?

Industry observers note that it is the first comprehensive molecular catalog of circulating blood proteins that are actively transported across the blood-brain barrier into the brain. Created by Gladstone Institutes researchers, the atlas identifies 92 specific plasma proteins (out of 861 tracked) that cross into the brain, primarily originating in peripheral organs such as the liver.

How does the “molecular ZIP code” system work?

The blood-brain barrier does not allow imported proteins to float around randomly. Once proteins cross the barrier, specialized molecular guidance cues direct them to specific cell types (such as astrocytes, neurons, or microglia) where they perform essential maintenance, such as protecting synaptic connections.

How does this discovery change our understanding of Alzheimer’s disease?

Scientists previously believed the blood-brain barrier’s primary fault in Alzheimer’s was becoming physically leaky. This study shows that before it ever leaks, the barrier stops importing vital protective proteins like APOA1 from the liver. Restoring these peripheral proteins reversed early signs of the disease, proving that neurodegeneration can be combated by repairing the body-to-brain supply line.

Adelson Medical Research Foundation, the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, the Larry L. Hillblom Foundation (2023-A-020-FEL), the National Science Foundation, and the NOMIS Foundation.

The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through path-ways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models.

Recent findings suggest that the blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma.

Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia.

In a recent development, this cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer’s risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake.

Recent findings suggest that hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

#48. Tech Report: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

Tech Report: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information.
  • However, a major new study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most crucial for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.
  • Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page.

However, a major new study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most crucial for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.

Sources indicate that dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties.

Massive Study Reveals What Really Predicts Reading Success.

Sources indicate that to investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions.

The findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing showed no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested.

Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly vital predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that "One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky said. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension.".

Two Overlooked Skills Play a Major Role in Reading.

It has been revealed that auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced.

Comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages.

Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles.

Recent findings suggest that the results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially important roles.

What the Findings Mean for Children Who Struggle to Read.

The research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs.

For families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support.

Recent findings suggest that "Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky mentioned. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together.".

The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home.

Sources indicate that according to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers.

#47. The Potential Benefits of Using an Anglo First Name

The Potential Benefits of Using an Anglo First Name

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Many Psychology Today readers are familiar with the dispiriting findings of studies conducted by social scientists: When they apply for jobs or housing, persons with ethnic minority names (like Lakeisha and Abdullah) are generally treated less well than persons with majority group names (like Daniel and Jennifer).
  • It has been revealed that will foreigners in the United States and Americans with foreign-sounding names be treated better if they adopt an Anglicized name?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Many Psychology Today readers are familiar with the dispiriting findings of studies conducted by social scientists: When they apply for jobs or housing, persons with ethnic minority names (like Lakeisha and Abdullah) are generally treated less well than persons with majority group names (like Daniel and Jennifer).

It has been revealed that will foreigners in the United States and Americans with foreign-sounding names be treated better if they adopt an Anglicized name? Would the immensely successful Nvidia executive Jensen Huang have been less successful in business if he had used his birth name, Jen-Hsun?

Two University of Kansas researchers, Xian Zhao and Monica Biernat, have conducted three studies that investigate the potential benefits that may accrue to foreigners who choose to use an Anglo name.

In the first study, 102 Americans—almost all of them White—looked at four photos of Chinese students who were attending college in the United States. Some participants saw photos that were labeled with an Anglo name like Andrew. Others saw photos that showed a Chinese name like Xiang. The participants used a 7-point scale to rate the similarity of each target “to Americans.”.

In a recent development, on average, the pictured individuals with Anglo names were rated as more similar to Americans, and the ones with Chinese names were rated as less similar. The difference wasn’t large—about a half-point on the 7-point scale—but it was statistically significant.

According to recent reports, in the second study, more than 400 college professors around the U.S. received an e-mail from “a student from China” who asked to meet and talk about the possibility of assisting with the professor’s research. Some professors received an e-mail in which the student introduced himself as Xian Zhao. Others received an e-mail in which the student introduced himself as “Xian Zhao, but you can call me by my English name Alex.” In every other way, the e-mail requests were identical.

Recent findings suggest that the different names affected the likelihood of getting a response. The “Alex” version received responses from 62 percent of the professors, while the “Xian” version received a response from just 53 percent.

Recent findings suggest that in the third study, 184 undergraduates—almost all of them White—listened to a four-minute mini-lecture about affective forecasting. The lecturer introduced himself as a student from China who was pursuing a doctorate in social psychology at the university. In one version of the recording, the lecturer stated, “Hi everyone. My name is Jian.” In another version, he said, “Hi everyone. My name is John” (an Anglicized version of Jian). In every other way, the recorded lectures were identical.

The participants were told to listen carefully to the lecture and then candidly evaluate the speaker because the department was “screening and selecting Ph.D. students to be instructors.” The participants also indicated the degree to which they support components of multiculturalism (wanting to learn from other cultural groups, for example) and the degree to which they believe that people who come to the United States should change their behavior to be more like Americans.

The participants evaluated the lecturer more favorably when he used an Anglo name and less favorably when he used his original Chinese name, but only among participants who rejected multiculturalism and believed foreigners should assimilate to local norms.

The opposite pattern was observed among participants who endorsed multiculturalism and did not endorse assimilationism. Those participants actually evaluated the lecturer more favorably when he used his original Chinese name.

The differences observed in these studies were not large, but the bottom line seems clear: Chinese students in the United States—and perhaps other international students—can potentially benefit by choosing to use an Anglo name, especially in more parochial parts of the country.

According to recent reports, this strategy, however, may also have a downside. In an earlier post, I reported the results of a 2018 study conducted by the same two Kansas researchers. In that study, Chinese students in the U.S. who adopted an Anglicized name reported slightly lower levels of self-esteem.

It has been revealed that it seems that adopting an Anglo name can be a double-edged sword for foreigners. Some employers may evaluate Jian Li slightly lower than John Lee, but Jian may feel somewhat better about himself than John does.

Zhao, X., & Biernat, M. (2017). Welcome to the U.S. but change your name? Adopting Anglo names and discrimination. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 70, 59-68.

#46. Now Yourself: The Elusive Science of What the Present Moment Is Made of and How It Makes You Who You Are

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2175 w)
